Its average, by contrast, is the ordinary difference-in-means DiD – averaging a quantile function returns a mean – so the information the curve adds is its shape, not its level.


The simple quantile-DiD above ignores covariate adjustment and bootstrap inference. Endid.jl adds both.

title: 12  Distributional Treatment Effects
section: 12.5 Beyond QTE: posterior bands as distributional output
text:
12.5 Beyond QTE: posterior bands as distributional output
TASC also produces more than a point estimate, but for a different object: the counterfactual path of one treated unit. QTE and TASC answer different questions:

QTE / Engression DiD: how does the treatment effect vary across the marginal distribution of outcomes when many units are treated?
TASC posterior band: how uncertain is the single counterfactual path when one unit is treated?

Use QTE when many treated units may have heterogeneous effects. Use TASC when the problem is a single treated unit with serial dependence.

title: 12  Distributional Treatment Effects
text:
12.6 Summary

ATE summarizes the mean. QTE summarizes changes across the outcome distribution.
QTE identification uses the same assumptions as ATE, but for CDFs.
Endid.jl estimates distributional DiD through Engression.
Report QTEs when the effect may differ across wages, test scores, health outcomes, sales, or other outcome distributions.

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
text:
13.1 \(T=2\) Panel Data
When unconfoundedness fails, we need weaker assumptions. The parallel trends assumption leads to the difference-in-differences estimator.
Suppose we have two periods, \(t = (1,2)\). Some units are treated just prior to period 2. For each individual \(i\), there are four potential outcomes:
\[ [Y_{i1}(0), Y_{i1}(1), Y_{i2}(0), Y_{i2}(1)]  \tag{13.1}\]
Let \(D\) denote the treated group. The ATT in period 2 is
\[ \tau_{2,att} = E(Y_2(1) - Y_2(0) | D=1)  \tag{13.2}\]
The first term is observed. The second is the counterfactual.

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
text:
13.2 Parallel Trends Assumption
\[ E[Y_2(0) -Y_1(0) | D=1] = E[Y_2(0) - Y_1(0) | D =0]  \tag{13.3}\]
or
\[ E[\Delta Y(0) | D=1] = E[\Delta Y(0) | D =0]  \tag{13.4}\]
In words, the change in untreated potential outcomes between periods 1 and 2 is the same for treated and control groups.

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
text:
13.3 No Anticipation Assumption
\[ E[Y_1(1) - Y_1(0) | D=1] = 0  \tag{13.5}\]
This is to say, in period 1, there is no treatment effect for the treated group.

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
section: 13.4 DiD is Identified with PT and NA
text:
13.4 DiD is Identified with PT and NA
With Parallel Trends, we notice \[\small  E[Y_2(0) | D=1 ]= E[Y_1(0) | D=1] + E[Y_2(0) - Y_1(0) | D=0]  \tag{13.6}\]
Then, with No Anticipation, \[
\begin{aligned}
E[Y_2(0) | D=1 ] &= E[Y_1(1) | D=1] + E[Y_2(0) - Y_1(0) | D=0]\\
&= E[Y_1 | D=1] + E[Y_2-Y_1 | D=0]
\end{aligned}
\tag{13.7}\]
\[\small  \tau_{2,att} = E[Y_2 - Y_1 | D=1] - E[Y_2-Y_1 | D=0]  \tag{13.8}\]
Parallel trends and no anticipation are the two assumptions we name, but they are not the whole set the derivation uses. It also maintains consistency and a well-defined treatment, so that \(Y = DY(1) + (1-D)Y(0)\) and the treatment has no hidden versions with different effects. It maintains no interference for the stated estimand: one unit’s outcome does not move with another unit’s treatment. Section 13.13 returns to this and shows what the estimand becomes when it fails. It maintains overlap, so both groups are observed in both periods and, once covariates enter, comparable units exist in each. And it maintains stable composition, so the same population is sampled in both periods. Differential attrition or entry breaks the comparison even when trends are parallel.

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
text:
13.5 Advantages and Disadvantages of DiD
Advantages:

No need to assume unconfoundedness. PT and NA take its place, alongside the maintained conditions listed above. Or say we don’t need treatment itself to be independent of potential outcomes, but we do need it to be independent to the change in potential outcome at least for untreated state. This is importantly weaker in a lot of situations. There can be selection bias. If the selection bias does not change over time, then DiD can handle it.

Disadvantages:

PT and NA might be violated.
PT is not scale free, in the sense that even if outcome can have PT, but then non-linear transformation of outcome won’t have PT (for example log of Y).

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
text:
13.6 Traditional DiD
In practice, DiD in many period setting is usually done with
\[ Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \phi_t + W_{it} \beta + \epsilon_{it}  \tag{13.9}\]
here \(W_{it} =(1[t=2] \cdot D_i)\), which is the interaction of post-treatment indicator and treatment group indicator.
This is usually called Two Way Fixed Effect (TWFE). There are multiple ways to implement the same model in practice.
TWFE can be done by “Pooled OLS”. That is, using OLS on time dummies and firm (individual) dummies. Wooldridge (2021) shows it’s equivalent to use treatment dummies, instead of individual dummies. He also shows that this model can be equivalently implemented with fixed effect model and random effect model.

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
text:
13.7 TWFE with Staggered Treatment Timing
The problem comes in when there is different timing of treatment. People used to still use
\[ Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \phi_t + W_{it} \beta + \epsilon_{it}  \tag{13.10}\]
where \(W_{it}\) now is a dummy when an individual \(i\) gets treated at time \(t\).
However, what is \(\beta\) here?

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
text:
13.8 Goodman-Bacon Decomposition
Goodman-Bacon (2021) showed that \(\beta\) in the TWFE is a weighted average of many different treatment effects, between treated cohorts, and control units, both can be different at different time points. The weights are a function of the size of the subsample, relative size of treatment and control units, and the timing of treatment in the sub sample. The decomposition weights themselves are non-negative and sum to one; the problem is that the units treated earlier are used as controls later. When those “forbidden” 2x2 comparisons are expressed in terms of the underlying cohort-time ATTs, some ATTs receive negative weight (de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille 2020). Therefore there is no meaningful interpretation of \(\beta\): it does not need to be a convex combination of treatment effects.



Bacon decomposition





Bacon decomposition

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
text:
13.9 Wooldridge’s ETWFE
There are a lot of ways to deal with staggered DiD situation. Wooldridge (2021) is basically saying: This is not a problem of TWFE, it’s a mis-use of TWFE. The reason we get non-sensible result of \(\beta\) is that we know there is heterogeneous treatment effect, in the sense the treatment effect differs across cohort, but we force them to be the same. If we relax it, it can work. As he shows, this works when we specify cohort effects accordingly.
\[ y_{it} = \alpha_i + \phi_t + \sum_{g=g_0}^G \sum_{t=g}^T \lambda_{g,t} \times 1(g,t) + \epsilon_{i,t}  \tag{13.11}\]
Here \(g\) is a cohort indicator, a cohort is determined by the time of getting treatment. ETWFE is allowing each cohort to have different effect at each different time point after being treated. The baseline group is the never treated group. If there is no never treated group, it can easily be changed to comparing to the last treated group.
When the treatment comes in amounts, such as a dose or a count, the same regression extends to it. The chapter DiD with Continuous Treatment covers that case.

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
text:
13.11 Example 2: Staggered DiD
To see whether ETWFE recovers what it should, we switch to simulated data where the answer is recorded in the file.
data/did_staggered_6.dta is Wooldridge’s simulated staggered panel: 500 units observed annually from 2001 to 2006, 3,000 observations. Units are treated in 2004 (119 units), 2005 (83) or 2006 (36), and 262 are never treated. The outcome is y, x is a covariate, d4, d5 and d6 are cohort dummies, and f04, f05, f06 are year dummies. What makes the file useful is te4, te5 and te6: the true unit-level treatment effect each unit would experience under each cohort’s treatment date. The effects are heterogeneous across units and grow with time since treatment, which is precisely the configuration that breaks plain TWFE.


Code

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
section: 13.12 Nonlinear ETWFE: Count and Binary Outcomes
text:
13.12 Nonlinear ETWFE: Count and Binary Outcomes

Related reading: The theory behind nonlinear ETWFE — Wooldridge’s conditional parallel-trends assumption on the linear index, the incidental parameters argument for cohort rather than unit intercepts, and the average partial effects that follow — is developed at length in Extended two-way fixed effects in Topics on Econometrics and Causal Inference, with count data and Poisson with exposure covering the count case in more detail.

ETWFE is not limited to linear (continuous) outcomes. When the dependent variable is a count or a binary indicator, linear TWFE can give nonsensical results — negative predicted probabilities, additive effects that ignore the bounded or non-negative nature of \(Y\). etwfe() supports the Poisson family via the family argument, which fits the model with fepois().
The key identifying assumption shifts slightly. Instead of parallel trends on \(E[Y_{it}(\infty)]\), we assume parallel trends on the linear index — that is, on \(\log E[Y_{it}(\infty)]\) for Poisson, or on \(\text{logit}\, E[Y_{it}(\infty)]\) for logit. This is Wooldridge’s (2023) Conditional Parallel Trends assumption stated on \(G^{-1}(E[Y])\). When the true treatment effect is multiplicative (e.g., a policy raises counts by 50% regardless of baseline), this assumption is more natural than additive PT on \(Y\) itself.
One implementation detail matters: the nonlinear ETWFE specification uses cohort fixed effects (one intercept per treatment cohort) plus year fixed effects — not individual unit fixed effects. etwfe() handles this automatically. In the linear case the two are numerically equivalent (Wooldridge 2021), but in nonlinear models unit fixed effects raise the incidental-parameters problem and make average partial effects uncomputable — the unit intercepts cannot be averaged out of the nonlinear link. Wooldridge (2023) instead uses cohort intercepts (a Mundlak device), which is what etwfe implements.

13.12.1 Simulated example: staggered count data
We simulate \(N = 400\) units over \(T = 6\) periods, 2,400 observations. Units are split into four groups of 100 by id: the first is treated from period 3, the second from period 4, the third from period 5, and the fourth never. Each unit draws a fixed effect \(\alpha_i \sim N(0, 0.3^2)\). The log mean is \(\log \mu_{it} = 1 + 0.2t + \alpha_i + 0.4 D_{it}\), and the outcome is \(Y_{it} \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_{it})\).
The treatment effect is multiplicative and homogeneous on the log scale: every treated unit’s expected count rises by a factor of \(\exp(0.4)\), that is by \(\exp(0.4) - 1 = 0.492\), or 49%. Parallel trends holds on the log scale by construction, and fails on the level scale, since a constant proportional effect is a larger absolute effect for units with higher baselines.
On the count scale the ATT is not 0.492. It is \(E[\mu_{it}(0) \mid \text{treated}] \times (\exp(0.4)-1)\), and the mean untreated count among treated observations is 7.518, so the true ATT is \(7.518 \times 0.4918 = 3.698\) counts.
The table below reports mean counts by cohort and treatment status.


Code
Random.seed!(42)
N = 400; Tmax = 6

unit_fe_vals = randn(N) .* 0.3

df_count = DataFrame([(id = i, year = t) for i in 1:N for t in 1:Tmax])
cohort_grp = ((df_count.id .- 1) .÷ 100) .+ 1
df_count.first_treat = [3, 4, 5, 0][cohort_grp]   # 0 = never treated
df_count.treated = (df_count.first_treat .> 0) .& (df_count.year .>= df_count.first_treat)
df_count.unit_fe = unit_fe_vals[df_count.id]
df_count.log_mu = 1 .+ 0.2 .* df_count.year .+ df_count.unit_fe .+ 0.4 .* df_count.treated
df_count.count = rand.(Poisson.(exp.(df_count.log_mu)))

# true count-scale ATT: mean untreated mean among treated observations times exp(0.4) - 1
mu0 = exp.(df_count.log_mu .- 0.4 .* df_count.treated)
@printf("mean untreated count among treated = %.3f, true ATT = %.3f\n",
        mean(mu0[df_count.treated]), mean(mu0[df_count.treated]) * (exp(0.4) - 1))

combine(groupby(df_count, [:first_treat, :treated]), :count => mean => :mean_count)

13.12.3 Event study

13.12.4 Comparison: linear ETWFE on log(count + 1)

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
text:
13.13 Spatial Interference
Everything in this chapter so far assumes SUTVA: one unit’s outcome does not depend on another unit’s treatment. That is not always plausible. A treated municipality may affect deforestation in nearby untreated municipalities. A vaccinated household may reduce transmission to nearby households. A labor-market policy in one commuting zone may change flows to its neighbors. With this kind of spatial spillover, the usual DiD estimand no longer has the interpretation we want. Xu (2023) shows that ignoring interference can produce an estimand that is neither a direct effect nor a spillover effect.
Xu (2023, 2026) develops a doubly robust DiD that keeps the identifying logic of conditional parallel trends but adds an exposure mapping \(G_{it} = G(i, W_{-it})\) for unit \(i\)’s neighborhood treatment status. The estimand is the direct ATT at exposure level \(g\),
\[ \tau_g(t, c) = \frac{1}{|S_M|} \sum_{i \in S_M} \mathbb{E}[y_{it}(c, g) - y_{it}(\infty, g) \mid z_i, C_i = c, G_{it} = g],  \tag{13.12}\]
where \(C_i\) is unit \(i\)’s first treatment period (so \(\{C_i > t\}\) is the not-yet-directly-treated comparison group), \(S_M = \{C_i = c\} \cup \{C_i > t\}\), and \(g\) is a chosen exposure level. The DR plug-in averages three pieces over \(S_M\): an IPW term from the treated cohort, an IPW term from the not-yet-treated, and a regression-imputation term, with three propensity models (\(\eta_{tc}\) for cohort, \(\eta_{tcg}\) and \(\eta_{t\infty g}\) for exposure) and two outcome-change regressions. It is consistent if either all three propensities or both outcome models are correctly specified.
The companion package DidInterference.jl implements this. The 2x2 base case (Xu 2023):


Code
using DidInterference, DataFrames

# Wide-format two-period data with a binary exposure G.
res = did_int_2x2(panel;
    yname      = :Y_post,
    yname_pre  = :Y_pre,
    treat      = :W,
    exposure   = :G,
    g          = 1,
    covariates = [:z1, :z2],
    trim       = 0.01)   # Xu (2026) uses 0.01 in the Brazil application

println(res.estimate, "  ", res.ci)


For staggered adoption (Xu 2026), did_int_staggered() loops over (cohort, time) cells with \(t \geq c\), restricts to \(S_M\) in each cell, fits the DR estimator, and aggregates across cells using joint-IF stacking (per-cell IFs share the never-treated comparison group, so independence-style SEs underestimate uncertainty noticeably). The R port didint has identical estimators; its vignettes/brazil_amazon.Rmd vignette replicates Section III of Xu (2026), the Lista de Municípios Prioritários policy on Amazon deforestation, using the public Assunção-McMillan-Murphy-Souza-Rodrigues replication archive on Zenodo.

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
text:
13.14 Persistent Outcomes and Heterogeneous Dynamics
Standard event-study TWFE regressions like
\[ Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \sum_{j} D_{it}^j \delta_j + X_{it}'\beta + U_{it}  \tag{13.13}\]
leave the dynamics of \(Y\) unmodelled. Three things get run together here and are worth separating.
The first is serial correlation in \(U_{it}\). That is an inference problem rather than an identification one: with exogenous treatment timing the event-time coefficients remain consistent, but conventional standard errors are wrong, which is why DiD is routinely clustered by unit.
The second is dynamic selection. If units are treated because of their recent outcomes, then treatment timing is related to lagged \(Y\) and the parallel-trends restriction the specification relies on no longer holds. That is an identification failure, and no amount of clustering repairs it.
The third is what motivates the rest of this section. When the outcome is genuinely persistent — earnings, employment, consumption, anything with habits or adjustment costs — the structural process carries its own lag, and Equation 13.13 is a static equation fitted to dynamic data. The event-time dummies then absorb the propagation of earlier shocks along with the treatment response, and the bias on those coefficients grows with the event-time horizon (Botosaru and Liu, 2025, Figure 1). Note where the bias comes from: not from persistence in the residual, which on its own does no such thing, but from fitting a static specification to a dynamic process.
Botosaru and Liu (2025) introduce a dynamic panel with correlated random coefficients that handles both persistence and unit-level heterogeneity in dynamic responses:
\[ Y_{it} = \rho_Y Y_{i,t-1} + \alpha_i + \sum_j D_{it}^j \delta_{ij} + X_{it}'\beta + U_{it},  \tag{13.14}\]
with a parsimonious AR(1) structure on the event-time effects to keep dimensionality manageable:
\[ \delta_{ij} = \rho_\delta \delta_{i,j-1} + \varepsilon_{ij}, \quad j \geq 1.  \tag{13.15}\]
The latent \(\lambda_i = (\alpha_i, \delta_{i0})\) is a unit-specific correlated random coefficient. A two-step semiparametric estimator: step 1 is quasi-maximum likelihood for the common parameters \((\rho_Y, \rho_\delta, \sigma_U^2, \sigma_\varepsilon^2, \beta)\) under a Gaussian working assumption on \(\lambda_i\) (consistent under misspecification of that working assumption); step 2 is Tweedie / Gaussian-conjugate empirical Bayes for the unit-level posterior trajectories \(\{\delta_{i,j}\}_{j=0}^J\), achieving asymptotic ratio optimality.
A companion paper (Botosaru and Liu 2026) adds a homogeneous-feedback extension: covariates \(X_{it}\) are allowed to adjust endogenously to past \(Y\) and treatment (the canonical example: minimum-wage policy affects wages directly and also indirectly through firms re-optimising input demand). Under the assumption that the covariate adjustment rule does not depend on \(\lambda_i\) given the observable history, the likelihood factors into a structural piece (for \(Y \mid X\), history) and a feedback piece (for \(X\) given history), each separately identified. The factorisation yields a clean decomposition of dynamic treatment effects into direct (through \(\delta_{i,j}\)) and indirect (through covariate feedback) components.
The package TVHTE.jl implements both papers:


Code
using TVHTE

# Fit on a panel with staggered cohorts and a covariate
fit = tvhte(panel_Y, baseline_Y; t0 = cohort, J = max_event_time, X = panel_X)

# Feedback model + direct/indirect counterfactual decomposition
fb = fit_feedback(panel_Y, baseline_Y, panel_X, baseline_X)
cf = simulate_counterfactual(fit, fb, alt_cohort)


An R port with the same API is at tvhte; both packages have deployed docs at https://xiangao.github.io/TVHTE.jl/ and https://xiangao.github.io/tvhte/.

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
text:
13.15 Synthetic Control and Synthetic DiD
The biggest problem with DiD is the PT assumption. Synthetic control and synthetic DiD replace it with weighted comparisons. The chapter Synthetic Control, DiD, and TASC covers both, with the California Proposition 99 example.

title: 13  Difference-in-Differences
text:
13.16 Summary
DiD replaces unconfoundedness with parallel trends and no anticipation. The untreated trend of the treated group is taken from the control group. With staggered timing, a single TWFE coefficient averages over comparisons that can use already-treated units as controls. ETWFE fixes this by giving each cohort its own effect in each period and then aggregating. A count outcome calls for the Poisson version, which assumes parallel trends on the log scale. Spillovers, persistent outcomes and a failure of parallel trends each need their own tools: interference-robust DiD, dynamic panels, and synthetic control or synthetic DiD, which the next chapter takes up.
On the minimum-wage data, ETWFE gives an ATT of \(-0.0506\) (0.0125). On Wooldridge’s simulated panel it returns 3.67 against a true 3.677. In the count simulation, Poisson ETWFE gives 3.62 (0.34) counts against a true 3.698, while linear ETWFE on \(\log(Y+1)\) returns 0.40, a number on a different scale.

title: 14  DiD with Continuous Treatment
text:
14.1 Two periods
The DiD chapter treats the treatment as on or off. Many treatments come in amounts. A county gets one Walmart or five. A state raises the minimum wage by fifty cents or by three dollars. A hospital receives a small grant or a large one. With a dose we want more than the effect of being treated. We want to know how the effect changes with the dose.
We first look at two periods, where Callaway, Goodman-Bacon, and Sant’Anna (2024), CGBS from here on, show what parallel trends identifies with a dose and what it leaves out. Two assumptions carry everything that follows: parallel trends and strong parallel trends. We then move to staggered adoption, using the heterogeneous-slopes extension of extended two-way fixed effects (ETWFE) in Wooldridge (2026), and replicate his study of Walmart and county retail employment.
We observe units \(i = 1, \dots, n\) in two periods, \(t = 1, 2\). Nobody is treated in period 1. Before period 2, each unit receives a dose \(D_i \ge 0\), and units with \(D_i = 0\) stay untreated. For each dose \(d\), unit \(i\) has a potential outcome \(Y_{it}(d)\), and we observe \(Y_{it} = Y_{it}(D_i)\). No anticipation means \(Y_{i1}(d) = Y_{i1}(0)\) for every \(d\). Let \(\Delta Y_i = Y_{i2} - Y_{i1}\).
There are two natural estimands. Take two doses \(d\) and \(d'\). The first estimand, \(ATT(d \mid d')\), is the average effect of dose \(d\), relative to no treatment, among the units that actually received dose \(d'\):
\[ATT(d \mid d') = E[Y_{i2}(d) - Y_{i2}(0) \mid D_i = d']. \tag{14.1}\]
The leading case is \(ATT(d \mid d)\), the effect of each group’s own dose. The second estimand, \(ATE(d)\), is the effect of dose \(d\) averaged over all treated units, whatever dose they received:
\[ATE(d) = E[Y_{i2}(d) - Y_{i2}(0) \mid D_i > 0]. \tag{14.2}\]
Its derivative \(ATE'(d)\) is the average causal response at \(d\): the average effect of a small increase in the dose.

title: 14  DiD with Continuous Treatment
text:
14.1.1 Parallel trends
The first assumption is parallel trends. With a dose it says that, without treatment, every dose group would have followed the trend of the untreated:
\[E[Y_{i2}(0) - Y_{i1}(0) \mid D_i = d] = E[Y_{i2}(0) - Y_{i1}(0) \mid D_i = 0] \quad \text{for all } d. \tag{14.3}\]
In words, the change in the untreated potential outcome between periods 1 and 2 is the same at every dose, including zero. The assumption restricts untreated outcomes only. Under Equation 14.3 and no anticipation,
\[E[\Delta Y_i \mid D_i = d] - E[\Delta Y_i \mid D_i = 0] = ATT(d \mid d). \tag{14.4}\]
This is the binary DiD done separately at each dose. Parallel trends identifies the whole curve \(ATT(d \mid d)\), each dose group’s effect of its own dose. With more periods before treatment we can check it in the usual way: the dose groups should have moved together before anyone was treated.
Parallel trends does not identify comparisons across doses. For the two doses \(d\) and \(d'\),
\[ATT(d \mid d) - ATT(d' \mid d') = \underbrace{ATT(d \mid d) - ATT(d' \mid d)}_{\text{causal response}} + \underbrace{ATT(d' \mid d) - ATT(d' \mid d')}_{\text{selection on gains}}. \tag{14.5}\]
The first term is causal. It is what moving the dose from \(d'\) to \(d\) does for the units that chose \(d\). The second term compares two groups at the same dose \(d'\). It is non-zero when the units that chose \(d\) would gain differently from dose \(d'\) than the units that chose \(d'\). Parallel trends says nothing about this term, and pre-treatment data cannot reveal it, because it involves treated outcomes. So the slope of the curve in Equation 14.4 mixes the causal response with selection on gains.


14.1.2 Strong parallel trends
The second assumption removes the selection term. CGBS call it strong parallel trends:
\[E[Y_{i2}(d) - Y_{i1}(0) \mid D_i = d] = E[Y_{i2}(d) - Y_{i1}(0) \mid D_i > 0] \quad \text{for all } d > 0. \tag{14.6}\]
In words, the average path from untreated in period 1 to dose \(d\) in period 2 is the same for the units that chose \(d\) as for all treated units. Together with Equation 14.3 it gives \(ATT(d \mid d) = ATE(d)\) for every \(d\): the average effect of a dose is the same in every dose group, whatever dose the group chose. The selection term in Equation 14.5 is then zero. Comparisons across doses are causal, and the slope of the identified curve is the average causal response.
Strong parallel trends is a stronger assumption than parallel trends, and of a different kind. It restricts treated potential outcomes, so no pre-treatment data can check it, and passing a pre-trend test says nothing about it. It restricts how units choose their dose. It is plausible when the dose is set for reasons unrelated to the gain, for example by a formula or a lottery. It is hard to defend when units choose their dose knowing what they will gain.
Wooldridge (2026) reaches the same point from a regression. Let \(B_i\) be the gain of unit \(i\) from one unit of dose, so that the effect is linear in the dose with a slope that varies across units: \(Y_{i2}(d) = Y_{i2}(0) + d B_i\). Let \(\gamma = E[Y_{i2}(0) - Y_{i1}(0)]\) be the untreated trend, and let \(\delta = E(B_i \mid D_i > 0)\) be the average slope among the treated. Under Equation 14.3,
\[E(\Delta Y_i \mid D_i) = \gamma + \delta D_i \tag{14.7}\]
holds when \(E(B_i \mid D_i = d) = \delta\) for every \(d > 0\). That condition is strong parallel trends for the linear model. Adding powers of \(D_i\) to the regression relaxes the linearity.

title: 14  DiD with Continuous Treatment
text:
14.2 Staggered adoption
Now units enter treatment at different times, as in the ETWFE section of the DiD chapter. Periods run \(t = 1, \dots, T\), and the first period in which any unit is treated is \(q\). A cohort \(g \in \{q, \dots, T\}\) is the set of units first treated in period \(g\). Let \(D_{ig} = 1\) if unit \(i\) is in cohort \(g\), and \(D_{ig} = 0\) otherwise. Never-treated units have \(D_{ig} = 0\) for every \(g\). The vector \(\mathbf D_i = (D_{iq}, \dots, D_{iT})\) collects unit \(i\)’s cohort dummies. For each period \(s\), the time dummy \(fs_t\) equals 1 if \(t = s\) and 0 otherwise.
The treatment \(\mathbf W_{it}\) is a \(1 \times J\) row vector, where \(J\) is the number of treatment variables. A single dose has \(J = 1\). A dose and its square has \(J = 2\). A set of mutually exclusive treatment levels has \(J\) equal to the number of levels. Every unit has \(\mathbf W_{it} = \mathbf 0\) before its entry period, and \(\mathbf W_i\) stacks unit \(i\)’s rows over all \(T\) periods. We write \(\mathbf w\) for a possible value of \(\mathbf W_{it}\). The dose may change after entry. In the Walmart data it is the number of stores open.
Wooldridge (2026) writes potential outcomes as linear in the treatment, with slopes that vary by unit and period. Let \(\mathbf B_{it}\) be a \(J \times 1\) vector of random slopes, whose \(j\)-th element is unit \(i\)’s gain in period \(t\) from one unit of treatment variable \(j\). Let \(\gamma_t\) be a time effect, \(C_i\) an unobserved unit effect, and \(U_{it}\) an idiosyncratic error. The potential outcome at treatment value \(\mathbf w\) is
\[Y_{it}(\mathbf w) = \mathbf w\, \mathbf B_{it} + \gamma_t + C_i + U_{it}. \tag{14.8}\]
For a single dose, \(J = 1\), write the scalar dose as \(w\). Subtracting the untreated potential outcome cancels the time effect, the unit effect and the error:
\[Y_{it}(w) - Y_{it}(0) = w\, B_{it}. \tag{14.9}\]
So \(B_{it}\) is the difference in potential outcomes per unit of dose. With several treatment variables, the \(j\)-th element of \(\mathbf B_{it}\) is the change in the potential outcome from one more unit of treatment variable \(j\), holding the others fixed. The additive \(\gamma_t + C_i\) is parallel trends. Nothing restricts \(\mathbf B_{it}\). The estimand is its mean for each cohort and period:
\[\boldsymbol\delta_{gs} = E(\mathbf B_{is} \mid D_{ig} = 1), \qquad s \ge g. \tag{14.10}\]
In words, \(\boldsymbol\delta_{gs}\) is the average effect per unit of each treatment variable for cohort \(g\) in period \(s\). Because the potential outcome is linear in the dose, it is also the effect of one more unit at any dose: going from 0 to 1 has the same effect as going from 1 to 2. Adding powers of the dose, or dummies for dose levels, to \(\mathbf W_{it}\) relaxes this. With a binary treatment, \(\boldsymbol\delta_{gs}\) is the cohort-period ATT of ETWFE.
Wooldridge assumes no anticipation and strict exogeneity. Strict exogeneity says the error \(U_{it}\) has mean zero given the whole treatment path \(\mathbf W_i\), the unit effect \(C_i\) and the slopes \(\mathbf B_{it}\). He needs one more assumption, which has no counterpart in the binary case. He calls it limited selection:
\[E(\mathbf B_{it} \mid \mathbf W_i) = E(\mathbf B_{it} \mid \mathbf D_i). \tag{14.11}\]
Once we know when a unit entered, its dose path carries no information about its average gain. With a binary treatment the entry date fixes the whole treatment path, so Equation 14.11 holds automatically. With two periods and a scalar dose it is the strong parallel trends of Equation 14.6 in its linear form. Parallel trends enters through the additive \(\gamma_t + C_i\) in Equation 14.8. So the staggered estimates rest on the same two assumptions as the two-period ones.
Let \(A_i = E(C_i \mid \mathbf W_i)\) be the mean of the unit effect given the treatment path. Under these assumptions,
\[E(Y_{it} \mid \mathbf W_i) = \sum_{g=q}^{T} \sum_{s=g}^{T} (D_{ig}\, fs_t\, \mathbf W_{it})\, \boldsymbol\delta_{gs} + \gamma_t + A_i. \tag{14.12}\]
\(A_i\) is a unit effect. So a two-way fixed effects (TWFE) regression of \(Y_{it}\) on the interactions \(D_{ig}\, fs_t\, \mathbf W_{it}\), with unit and time effects, estimates every \(\boldsymbol\delta_{gs}\). This is ETWFE with the treatment indicator replaced by the dose. Standard errors are clustered by unit.
There are many cohort-period slopes, so we aggregate them. Let \(e\) be the exposure time, the number of periods since entry, and let \(N_g\) be the number of units in cohort \(g\). Let \(\hat{\boldsymbol\delta}_{gs}\) be the TWFE estimate of \(\boldsymbol\delta_{gs}\). The estimated effect at exposure \(e\), written \(\hat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{e}\), averages over the cohorts observed that long, with weights proportional to cohort size:
\[\hat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{e} = \sum_{g=q}^{T-e} \frac{N_g}{N_q + \dots + N_{T-e}}\, \hat{\boldsymbol\delta}_{g,g+e}. \tag{14.13}\]
The overall effect weights every cohort-period slope by \(N_g\). In a balanced panel it is the average slope over all treated unit-periods.
Pre-trends can be tested in two ways. A lead is a dummy \(D_{ig}\, fs_t\) for a period \(s\) before cohort \(g\) enters. The first test fits TWFE on the untreated observations only, the unit-periods with \(\mathbf W_{it} = \mathbf 0\), with leads for \(s \le g - 2\), so that the period just before entry is the base. It then tests whether the leads are zero. The second test adds the same leads to Equation 14.12. With a binary treatment the two give identical estimates. With a dose they differ. Both tests check parallel trends. Neither checks limited selection. When the leads show a trend, Wooldridge adds cohort-specific linear trends to Equation 14.12. For each cohort \(g\), the regressor \(D_{ig} \cdot t\) is a linear time trend for that cohort only. The assumption then becomes that each cohort’s gap from the never-treated units would have kept growing along the same line after entry.

title: 14  DiD with Continuous Treatment
section: 14.3 Wooldridge’s regression and the CGBS estimator
text:
14.3 Wooldridge’s regression and the CGBS estimator
The two approaches target the same objects. Under parallel trends and strong parallel trends, each identifies the average effect of the dose for every cohort and period. They differ in how they estimate it and in what they can handle.
The first difference is the comparison group. Wooldridge runs one TWFE regression in levels on all periods, Equation 14.12. Every untreated observation serves as a control: the never-treated units, the not-yet-treated units, and the pre-entry periods of every cohort. In the binary case this regression is the imputation estimator of Borusyak, Jaravel, and Spiess (2024). Callaway, Goodman-Bacon, and Sant’Anna (2024) build on Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) instead. For each cohort and period they compare the cohort with the never-treated or the not-yet-treated units, using the long difference from the period just before entry, and fit the dose response in that comparison. The regression uses more data, and it is more efficient when the errors are homoskedastic and serially uncorrelated. In exchange it needs parallel trends in every pre-entry period. The differencing approach needs it only from the base period on.
The second difference is the shape of the dose response. In Wooldridge’s regression, the shape comes from the functions of the dose placed in \(\mathbf W_{it}\): the dose itself, its powers, or dummies for dose levels. The estimand is the average slope \(\boldsymbol\delta_{gs}\). CGBS fit a B-spline in the dose within each cohort and period, or a nonparametric curve whose complexity is chosen from the data. They report the curve \(ATT(d \mid d)\) and its derivative. The two also treat a dose near zero differently. With two periods, Wooldridge’s regression has no separate intercept for the treated units, so its fitted effect goes to zero as the dose goes to zero. The CGBS fit gives the treated units their own intercept, so the effect can jump at any positive dose. The two coincide once a dummy for a positive dose is added to \(\mathbf W_{it}\).
The third difference is scope. The table compares Wooldridge’s regression with the R package contdid, version 0.1.1, which implements CGBS.

One more Walmart raises retail employment by 3.4%, with a standard error of 0.57 percentage points. In the binary case this regression makes forbidden comparisons, which use already-treated units as controls, when effects vary by cohort and time. The same holds with a dose. So we build the regressors of Equation 14.12, one for each cohort and year from entry on: \(W_{it}\) times the cohort dummy times the year dummy.


Code
cohorts = 1986:1999
cells = [(g, s) for g in cohorts for s in cohorts if s >= g]
wcols = [Symbol("w_$(g)_$(s)") for (g, s) in cells]
for ((g, s), c) in zip(cells, wcols)
    wm[!, c] = (wm.cohort .== g) .* (wm.year .== s) .* wm.n_open
end
trcols = [Symbol("tr_$g") for g in cohorts]
for (g, c) in zip(cohorts, trcols)
    wm[!, c] = (wm.cohort .== g) .* wm.year
end

fit_het = feols(wm, term(:log_retail_emp) ~ sum(term.(wcols)) + fe(:fips) + fe(:year),
                vcov = Vcov.cluster(:fips))
length(coef(fit_het))


105


That gives 105 slopes. We aggregate them with Equation 14.13. Each aggregate is a linear combination of the slopes with fixed weights, so its standard error comes from the clustered covariance matrix. This matches Stata’s margins in Wooldridge’s code.


Code
Ng = Dict(g => sum((wm.year .== 1999) .& (wm.cohort .== g)) for g in cohorts)

function aggregate_slopes(fit)
    pos = Dict(n => i for (i, n) in enumerate(coefnames(fit)))
    b = coef(fit); V = vcov(fit)
    lincomb(a) = (dot(a, b), sqrt(a' * V * a))
    out = map(0:13) do e
        gs = [g for g in cohorts if g + e <= 1999]
        a = zeros(length(b))
        for g in gs
            a[pos["w_$(g)_$(g + e)"]] = Ng[g] / sum(Ng[h] for h in gs)
        end
        lincomb(a)
    end
    a = zeros(length(b))
    for (g, s) in cells
        a[pos["w_$(g)_$(s)"]] = Ng[g]
    end
    push!(out, lincomb(a ./ sum(a)))
end
agg_het = aggregate_slopes(fit_het);


Before reading the effects, we check pre-trends. Following the first test above, we fit TWFE on the untreated county-years with a lead for each cohort and each year at least two years before entry. We then average the leads by years until entry, with the cohort weights of Equation 14.13.


Code
un = wm[wm.n_open .== 0, [:fips, :year, :cohort, :log_retail_emp]]
leads = [(g, s) for g in cohorts for s in 1977:1999 if s <= g - 2]
lcols = [Symbol("l_$(g)_$(s)") for (g, s) in leads]
for ((g, s), c) in zip(leads, lcols)
    un[!, c] = Float64.((un.cohort .== g) .& (un.year .== s))
end
fit_pre = feols(un, term(:log_retail_emp) ~ sum(term.(lcols)) + fe(:fips) + fe(:year),
                vcov = Vcov.cluster(:fips))
pos = Dict(n => i for (i, n) in enumerate(coefnames(fit_pre)))
b = coef(fit_pre); V = vcov(fit_pre)
pre = DataFrame(map(2:22) do k
    gs = [g for g in cohorts if g - k >= 1977]
    a = zeros(length(b))
    for g in gs
        a[pos["l_$(g)_$(g - k)"]] = Ng[g] / sum(Ng[h] for h in gs)
    end
    (time = -k, estimate = dot(a, b), se = sqrt(a' * V * a))
end)

fig = Figure(size = (700, 360))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Years until first Walmart", ylabel = "Log retail employment")
hlines!(ax, 0, color = :black)
rangebars!(ax, pre.time, pre.estimate .- 1.96 .* pre.se, pre.estimate .+ 1.96 .* pre.se,
           color = :darkcyan)
scatter!(ax, pre.time, pre.estimate, color = :darkcyan)
fig



Weighted pre-treatment estimates from the untreated observations, with 95% intervals. The year before entry is the base.

Twenty years before entry, counties that later got a Walmart had retail employment about 19 log points lower, relative to the year before entry, than the never-treated counties. The table reproduces Table 7.1 of Wooldridge (2026), estimates and standard errors, to all four decimals.
Without trends, one more store raises retail employment by about 3% to 4% in the first years. The effect climbs to 9% by year 13. The overall effect is 0.0386 (0.0051). It is close to the single-coefficient TWFE estimate of 0.0344, and a little more precise.
The cohort trends change the estimates a lot. The effect in the entry year is 0.0049 (0.0033), indistinguishable from zero. From the entry year to year 6, the effects are between a sixth and a half of their values without trends. They then rise steadily, and by year 13 the two columns agree at about 0.09. The overall effect falls to 0.0156 (0.0046), less than half the estimate without trends. The trends also make the estimates more precise up to about year 8. The long exposures rest on the earliest cohorts only, so their standard errors grow. Year 13 comes from the 1986 cohort alone.
For comparison, we add the same 14 cohort trends to the single-coefficient regression. One slope on the store count is then shared by every cohort and year.

The figure plots the estimated effect of one store, \(\hat\delta_{1990,s}\), for each year after entry, with and without cohort trends. The effect of two stores is twice as large in every year, because the model is linear in the dose.


Code
g0 = 1990
nm = ["w_$(g0)_$(s)" for s in g0:1999]
fig = Figure(size = (700, 360))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Years since the first Walmart opened",
          ylabel = "Effect of one store", xticks = 0:9)
hlines!(ax, 0, color = :black)
for (fit, label, shift, col) in [(fit_het, "No trends", -0.12, :darkcyan),
                                 (fit_trend, "Cohort trends", 0.12, :darkorange)]
    pos = Dict(n => i for (i, n) in enumerate(coefnames(fit)))
    idx = [pos[n] for n in nm]
    est = coef(fit)[idx]; se = sqrt.(diag(vcov(fit))[idx])
    x = (0:9) .+ shift
    rangebars!(ax, x, est .- 1.96 .* se, est .+ 1.96 .* se, color = col)
    scatter!(ax, x, est, color = col, label = label)
end
Legend(fig[2, 1], ax, orientation = :horizontal, framevisible = false)
fig



Effect of one Walmart on log retail employment in the 1990 cohort, by year since entry, with 95% intervals.


Without trends, one store raises retail employment in the 1990 cohort by 1.7% in the entry year and by 4.0% a year later, and the effect then settles near 2.7%. From year 1 on, the estimates are about twice their standard errors or more. With cohort trends the path is lower, and the gap grows from 0.6 percentage points in the entry year to 1.6 by year 9. Only the year-1 estimate, 3.1%, is more than twice its standard error. The growing gap is what we would see if the cohort trend, which is also fit on post-entry years, absorbs part of an effect that grows with exposure. The plot holds the dose at one store. The cohort’s average number of stores rises from 1.08 in 1990 to 1.75 in 1999, so the effect it actually experienced grows faster than the plotted per-store effect.

title: 14  DiD with Continuous Treatment
text:
14.5 Summary
Wooldridge’s method is ETWFE with the treatment indicator replaced by the dose. The regression in Equation 14.12 interacts cohort, year and dose. Each interaction has its own slope \(\boldsymbol\delta_{gs}\), the average effect of one more unit of dose for cohort \(g\) in year \(s\), and the slopes are averaged by exposure time. Covariates, cohort trends, exit and unbalanced panels enter as extra terms in the same regression.
Two assumptions identify the slopes. Parallel trends lets us compare each cohort’s change with the change of the untreated units, and the pre-trend tests check it. Strong parallel trends, which Wooldridge’s limited selection extends to staggered adoption, says the dose a unit ends up with tells us nothing about its average gain. It makes comparisons across doses causal, and no test in the data checks it. In the Walmart data parallel trends fails, so we add cohort trends, and the overall effect of one more store falls from 3.9% to 1.6%.




Borusyak, Kirill, Xavier Jaravel, and Jann Spiess. 2024. “Revisiting Event Study Designs: Robust and Efficient Estimation.” Review of Economic Studies 91 (6): 3253–85.


Brown, Nicholas, and Kyle Butts. 2025. “Dynamic Treatment Effect Estimation with Interactive Fixed Effects and Short Panels.” Journal of Econometrics 250: 106013.


Callaway, Brantly, Andrew Goodman-Bacon, and Pedro H. C. Sant’Anna. 2024. “Difference-in-Differences with a Continuous Treatment.” NBER Working Paper 32117. National Bureau of Economic Research. https://doi.org/10.3386/w32117.


Callaway, Brantly, and Pedro H. C. Sant’Anna. 2021. “Difference-in-Differences with Multiple Time Periods.” Journal of Econometrics 225 (2): 200–230.


Wooldridge, Jeffrey M. 2026. “A Heterogeneous Slopes Approach to Difference-in-Differences with Non-Binary Treatments.” SSRN Working Paper 7530698.

title: 15  Synthetic Control, DiD, and TASC
text:
15.1 Synthetic Control
Here I put three related panel-data designs together: classical synthetic control, synthetic DiD, and Time-Aware Synthetic Control (TASC). All compare a treated unit to a donor pool over time. They differ in what structure they put on the untreated counterfactual.
The biggest problem with DiD is the parallel trends assumption. There is not really a test for it, just like the unconfoundedness assumption. It is less demanding than unconfoundedness, but it is still hard to justify in many applications.
Synthetic control starts from a different idea. Instead of giving every control unit the same weight, it constructs a synthetic control unit from the donor pool:
\[
\hat Y_{1t}(0) = \sum_{i=2}^{N} \hat \omega_i Y_{it},
\tag{15.1}\]
where the weights are chosen to make the synthetic unit close to the treated unit before treatment. The usual Abadie-style version restricts the donor weights to be nonnegative and to sum to one. The identifying hope is not that the average control follows the treated unit, but that some weighted average of controls does.
Classical synthetic control is time-agnostic in an important sense: the pre-treatment periods enter the weight-fitting problem as a set of matching moments. If we permute the order of the pre-treatment periods, the fitted donor weights are unchanged. This is often a strength because it avoids imposing a time-series model, but it can leave predictive information unused when there is a stable trend.
crumbs: 15  Synthetic Control, DiD, and TASC

title: 15  Synthetic Control, DiD, and TASC
text:
15.2 Synthetic DiD
Arkhangelsky et al. (2021) combine the idea of DiD and synthetic control. Standard DiD assigns equal weight to all control units and all pre-treatment time periods. Synthetic control assigns data-driven weights to donor units. Synthetic DiD uses both unit weights and time weights.
The three estimators below are written as a unifying weighted-regression sketch: the same two-way fixed-effect regression, with different weights switched on. This is a useful way to see how DiD, synthetic control, and synthetic DiD relate, but it is not the estimators’ actual optimization problems. In particular, the synthetic-control weights \(\hat\omega_i^{sc}\) are not free regression weights — in Abadie’s formulation they are chosen by a separate optimization that matches pre-treatment outcomes (and predictors) of the treated unit, subject to \(\omega_i \ge 0,\ \sum_i \omega_i = 1\). Likewise the SDID unit and time weights \(\hat\omega_i^{sdid}, \hat\lambda_t^{sdid}\) come from their own penalized pre-period optimization problems. Treat the displays below as schematic; see the package documentation (or Arkhangelsky et al. 2021) for the exact weight-selection problems.
The DiD objective can be written as
\[
\small
(\hat \tau^{did}, \hat \mu, \hat \alpha, \hat \beta)
= \underset{\tau, \mu, \alpha, \beta}{\arg\min}
\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^T
(Y_{it} - \mu - \alpha_i - \beta_t - W_{it}\tau)^2.
\tag{15.2}\]
Synthetic control can be viewed as a weighted version that puts the donor weights into the comparison:
\[
\small
(\hat \tau^{sc}, \hat \mu, \hat \beta)
= \underset{\tau, \mu, \beta}{\arg\min}
\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^T
(Y_{it} - \mu - \beta_t - W_{it}\tau)^2 \hat \omega_i^{sc}.
\tag{15.3}\]
Synthetic DiD adds time weights:
\[
\small
(\hat \tau^{sdid}, \hat \mu, \hat \alpha, \hat \beta)
= \underset{\tau, \mu, \alpha, \beta}{\arg\min}
\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^T
(Y_{it} - \mu - \alpha_i - \beta_t - W_{it}\tau)^2
\hat \omega_i^{sdid}\hat \lambda_t^{sdid}.
\tag{15.4}\]
The unit weights try to make the donor pool look like the treated unit. The time weights put more emphasis on pre-treatment periods that are more informative about the post-treatment period.
crumbs: 15  Synthetic Control, DiD, and TASC

title: 15  Synthetic Control, DiD, and TASC
text:
15.3 Time-Aware Synthetic Control
TASC was proposed by Rho et al. (2026). It starts from the same panel-data structure, but it models the donor and treated outcomes through a latent time-series system:
\[
x_t = A x_{t-1} + q_t,\qquad q_t \sim N(0,Q),
\tag{15.5}\]
\[
y_t = Hx_t + r_t,\qquad r_t \sim N(0,R).
\tag{15.6}\]
Here \(y_t\) is the vector of outcomes across units at time \(t\), and \(x_t\) is a low-dimensional latent state. The matrix \(H\) maps the latent state into unit outcomes, so \(HX\) is a low-rank signal. The matrix \(A\) is the new piece relative to classical synthetic control: it says that the latent time factors evolve according to a stable trend.
The counterfactual step is simple. TASC learns the state-space model from the pre-treatment panel. After treatment, the treated unit’s observed outcome is treated as missing. The filter and smoother continue to use the donor units to infer the latent state, and the treated row of \(H\) maps that state into the untreated counterfactual:
\[
\hat Y_{1t}(0) = h_1^\top \hat x_t,\qquad t > T_0.
\tag{15.7}\]
The estimated treatment effect is then
\[
\hat \tau_t = Y_{1t} - \hat Y_{1t}(0).
\tag{15.8}\]
Relative to classical synthetic control, TASC uses the order of time. Relative to synthetic DiD, it puts the time dependence in a generative latent-state model rather than in a set of pre-period weights. This can help when trends are stable and outcomes are noisy, but it is also a stronger modeling assumption.
crumbs: 15  Synthetic Control, DiD, and TASC

title: 15  Synthetic Control, DiD, and TASC
text:
15.4 Example: California Proposition 99
California’s Proposition 99 raised cigarette taxes and funded anti-smoking programs. The usual synthetic-control exercise compares California’s cigarette sales after 1988 to a donor pool of other states. The outcome is per-capita cigarette sales in packs.


Code
california = california_prop99()
setup = panel_matrices(california, :State, :Year, :PacksPerCapita, :treated)

tau_sdid = synthdid_estimate(setup.Y, setup.N0, setup.T0)
tau_sc   = sc_estimate(setup.Y, setup.N0, setup.T0)
tau_did  = did_estimate(setup.Y, setup.N0, setup.T0)
nothing


SynthDiD.jl orders the donor states first and treated states last. TASC.jl expects the treated unit to be first, so we explicitly reorder the matrix before fitting the state-space model. The paper’s Proposition 99 example uses a low latent dimension; here we set d = 2.


Code
Y_tasc = vcat(setup.Y[(setup.N0 + 1):end, :], setup.Y[1:setup.N0, :])

tasc_model = fit_tasc(
    Y_tasc;
    d = 2,
    T0 = setup.T0,
    n_em = 200,
    tol = 1e-3,
)

tasc_pred = predict_counterfactual(tasc_model, Y_tasc)
tasc_att = mean(tasc_pred.effect[(setup.T0 + 1):end])
nothing




Code
estimates = DataFrame(
    Method = ["Diff-in-Diff", "Synthetic Control", "Synthetic Diff-in-Diff", "TASC"],
    Estimate = [tau_did.estimate, tau_sc.estimate, tau_sdid.estimate, tasc_att],
)

DataFrames.transform(estimates, :Estimate => ByRow(x -> round(x, digits = 2)) => :EstimateRounded)

The estimates are all negative: California’s observed cigarette sales fell below the estimated no-Proposition-99 counterfactual. The methods differ because they impose different restrictions on the untreated path. DiD compares average changes. Synthetic control chooses donor weights. Synthetic DiD adds time weights. TASC uses a low-rank state-space model and updates the latent state with post-treatment donor observations.


Code
years = Int.(setup.times)
treated = vec(setup.Y[(setup.N0 + 1), :])
sc_counterfactual = vec(tau_sc.weights.omega' * setup.Y[1:setup.N0, :])
# SynthDiD fits with omega_intercept=true, so its synthetic match is c + ω'Y_donors
# for a fitted level shift c (the omega weights demean the donor columns). Add the
# pre-period level shift back so the plotted line matches the path SynthDiD compares
# the treated unit against; otherwise the line is vertically offset.
sdid_raw = vec(tau_sdid.weights.omega' * setup.Y[1:setup.N0, :])
sdid_intercept = mean(treated[1:setup.T0]) - mean(sdid_raw[1:setup.T0])
sdid_counterfactual = sdid_raw .+ sdid_intercept
tasc_counterfactual = tasc_pred.target
tasc_se = sqrt.(max.(tasc_pred.variance, 0.0))
tasc_lower = tasc_counterfactual .- 1.96 .* tasc_se
tasc_upper = tasc_counterfactual .+ 1.96 .* tasc_se

fig = Figure(size = (760, 430))
ax = Axis(
    fig[1, 1],
    xlabel = "Year",
    ylabel = "Packs per capita",
    title = "California Proposition 99: Counterfactual Paths",
)

band!(ax, years, tasc_lower, tasc_upper, color = (:seagreen, 0.18), label = "TASC 95% interval")
lines!(ax, years, treated, color = :black, linewidth = 3, label = "California")
lines!(ax, years, sc_counterfactual, color = :steelblue, linewidth = 2, label = "SC")
lines!(ax, years, sdid_counterfactual, color = :darkorange, linewidth = 2, label = "SynthDiD")
lines!(ax, years, tasc_counterfactual, color = :seagreen, linewidth = 2, label = "TASC")
vlines!(ax, years[setup.T0] + 0.5, color = :gray40, linestyle = :dash)

axislegend(ax, position = :lb)
fig





The figure emphasizes where the counterfactual enters. After 1988, the black line is observed California. The colored lines are estimates of California’s untreated path. The treatment-effect path is the vertical gap between the black line and each counterfactual.

title: 15  Synthetic Control, DiD, and TASC
text:
15.5 Summary
All three designs compare a treated unit with a donor pool over time. They differ in the structure they put on the untreated path. Synthetic control replaces parallel trends with a weighted average of donors chosen to match the treated unit before treatment. Synthetic DiD adds time weights that favour the pre-treatment periods most like the post-treatment ones. TASC models outcomes through a low-rank latent state that evolves over time, so it uses the order of time that synthetic control ignores. That is a stronger modelling assumption, and it helps when trends are stable and outcomes are noisy.
For Proposition 99 all four estimates are negative: \(-27.35\) for DiD, \(-19.62\) for synthetic control, \(-15.60\) for synthetic DiD and \(-17.11\) for TASC. Each says California’s cigarette sales fell below its estimated counterfactual. The spread across methods reflects their different restrictions on the untreated path.




Rho, Saeyoung, Cyrus Illick, Samhitha Narasipura, Alberto Abadie, Daniel Hsu, and Vishal Misra. 2026. “Time-Aware Synthetic Control.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2601.03099. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03099.
crumbs: 15  Synthetic Control, DiD, and TASC

title: 16  Randomization Inference for Synthetic Control
text:
16.1 The placebo test
Synthetic control is often used when there is one treated unit: California, West Germany, the Basque Country. Usual large-sample standard errors are not very helpful because there is no large sample of treated units. Two approaches are common:
Here I use both on the Proposition 99 panel.
The placebo idea is simple. Take each control unit in turn, pretend it was treated, and re-run synthetic control. This produces a placebo gap for each donor. The collection of placebo gaps is a reference distribution: it shows how large a gap this estimator returns for a unit we are prepared to treat as exchangeable with California. It becomes an empirical null distribution only if that exchangeability can be defended. In an observational setting that is an assumption, not something the data supply.
If California’s gap is large relative to the placebo gaps, that is evidence against the no-effect null.
Code
california = california_prop99()
setup = panel_matrices(california, :State, :Year, :PacksPerCapita, :treated)
Y    = setup.Y
N0   = setup.N0           # 38 donor states
T0   = setup.T0           # 1989 onward is post-treatment
N1   = size(Y, 1) - N0    # 1 treated state (California)
years = Int.(setup.times)

# California's observed effect (SC estimate)
tau_sc = sc_estimate(Y, N0, T0)
ca_obs = vec(Y[N0 + 1, :])
ca_cfact = vec(tau_sc.weights.omega' * Y[1:N0, :])
ca_effect = mean(ca_obs[(T0 + 1):end]) - mean(ca_cfact[(T0 + 1):end])

@printf("California ATT (SC): %.2f packs per capita\n", ca_effect)


California ATT (SC): -19.62 packs per capita
Now run the placebo: each control state takes a turn as the “treated” unit.
Code
function run_placebo(Y, N0, T0, treated_idx)
    # Swap treated_idx into the last row (treated slot); remaining donors fill 1..N0-1
    donor_idx = setdiff(1:N0, treated_idx)
    Y_perm    = vcat(Y[donor_idx, :], Y[treated_idx:treated_idx, :])
    fit       = sc_estimate(Y_perm, length(donor_idx), T0)
    treated   = vec(Y_perm[end, :])
    cfact     = vec(fit.weights.omega' * Y_perm[1:length(donor_idx), :])
    return treated, cfact
end

placebo_effects = Float64[]
placebo_paths   = Matrix{Float64}(undef, N0, size(Y, 2))
placebo_cfacts  = Matrix{Float64}(undef, N0, size(Y, 2))

for i in 1:N0
    treated_i, cfact_i = run_placebo(Y, N0, T0, i)
    placebo_paths[i, :]  = treated_i .- cfact_i
    placebo_cfacts[i, :] = cfact_i
    push!(placebo_effects, mean(treated_i[(T0 + 1):end] .- cfact_i[(T0 + 1):end]))
end

# California's treatment effect path
ca_gap = ca_obs .- ca_cfact

@printf("California ATT:        %.2f\n", ca_effect)
@printf("Placebo distribution mean: %.2f\n", mean(placebo_effects))
@printf("Placebo distribution sd:   %.2f\n", std(placebo_effects))


California ATT:        -19.62
Placebo distribution mean: 0.32
Placebo distribution sd:   10.76

title: 16  Randomization Inference for Synthetic Control
text:
16.1.1 The two-sided p-value
A Fisher-style exact \(p\)-value is the fraction of placebo effects at least as extreme (in absolute value) as the observed effect:


Code
# Fisher exact convention: count California itself in numerator and denominator,
# so the p-value floor is 1/(N0+1) = 1/39 rather than 0.
p_value = (1 + sum(abs.(placebo_effects) .>= abs(ca_effect))) / (length(placebo_effects) + 1)
@printf("Two-sided p-value: %.3f\n", p_value)


Two-sided p-value: 0.077


With 38 donor states, the smallest possible \(p\)-value is \(1/39 \approx 0.026\) (California plus 38 placebos). A \(p\)-value at this floor means the observed effect is more extreme than every placebo.
Call it an exact randomization \(p\)-value only when an assignment mechanism earns the word. Exactness needs the treated label to be exchangeable across the 39 units under the null, and it needs the estimator reapplied symmetrically to each of them. Proposition 99 was not randomly assigned to California. Nothing in the design delivers that exchangeability, California differs from most donors in size, and its assignment probability was not \(1/39\). Abadie (2021) makes the point directly: the procedure reduces to classical randomization inference when treatment is randomly assigned, which is an unusual situation in aggregate observational applications. Absent that argument, read the number as an in-space placebo diagnostic, a measure of how unusual California looks among the donors. Ferman and Pinto (2017) show separately that placebo tests can be distorted in size when pre-treatment fit varies across units and the weights are estimated.


16.1.2 The placebo plot
The usual plot overlays the placebo gaps in grey and California’s gap in black. If the black line is outside the grey cloud, California looks unusual.


Code
fig = Figure(size = (740, 380), fontsize = 13)
ax  = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Year", ylabel = "Gap: observed − synthetic",
           title = "Placebo gap trajectories")
for i in 1:N0
    lines!(ax, years, placebo_paths[i, :],
           color = (:grey, 0.35), linewidth = 1)
end
lines!(ax, years, ca_gap, color = :black, linewidth = 2.5, label = "California")
hlines!(ax, [0.0]; color = :gray40, linestyle = :dot, linewidth = 1)
vlines!(ax, [years[T0] + 0.5]; color = :gray40, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 1)
axislegend(ax, position = :lb, framevisible = false)
fig



California’s treatment-effect gap (black) vs placebo gaps from each donor state (grey). The vertical dashed line marks 1989.
crumbs: 16  Randomization Inference for Synthetic Control

title: 16  Randomization Inference for Synthetic Control
text:
16.2 The MSPE ratio test
Some donor states fit California’s pre-period trajectory better than others. A placebo state whose synthetic control fits its own pre-period poorly will produce a large pre-period gap by construction, inflating its placebo effect even under the sharp null. Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller (2015) propose normalising by pre-treatment fit:
\[
\text{MSPE ratio}(\ell) = \frac{\frac{1}{T - T_0}\sum_{t > T_0} (Y_{\ell t} - \hat Y_{\ell t})^2}
                              {\frac{1}{T_0}\sum_{t \le T_0} (Y_{\ell t} - \hat Y_{\ell t})^2}.
\tag{16.1}\]
A large ratio means post-treatment gap is large relative to pre-treatment fit. The MSPE ratio test compares California’s ratio to the distribution of placebo ratios.


Code
function mspe_ratio(treated, cfact, T0)
    pre  = mean((treated[1:T0] .- cfact[1:T0]).^2)
    post = mean((treated[(T0 + 1):end] .- cfact[(T0 + 1):end]).^2)
    return post / max(pre, eps())
end

ca_ratio = mspe_ratio(ca_obs, ca_cfact, T0)

placebo_ratios = Float64[]
for i in 1:N0
    treated_i, cfact_i = run_placebo(Y, N0, T0, i)
    push!(placebo_ratios, mspe_ratio(treated_i, cfact_i, T0))
end

p_ratio = (1 + sum(placebo_ratios .>= ca_ratio)) / (length(placebo_ratios) + 1)
@printf("California MSPE ratio: %.2f\n", ca_ratio)
@printf("Placebo ratio 75th pct: %.2f\n", quantile(placebo_ratios, 0.75))
@printf("Placebo ratio max:     %.2f\n", maximum(placebo_ratios))
@printf("One-sided p-value (ratio): %.3f\n", p_ratio)


California MSPE ratio: 154.94
Placebo ratio 75th pct: 35.00
Placebo ratio max:     536.00
One-sided p-value (ratio): 0.077


The MSPE ratio discounts placebo states that were poorly fit before treatment.


Code
fig = Figure(size = (640, 360), fontsize = 13)
ax  = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Post/Pre MSPE ratio",
           ylabel = "Count", title = "MSPE ratio distribution")
hist!(ax, placebo_ratios, bins = 20, color = (:steelblue, 0.6))
vlines!(ax, [ca_ratio]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2, linestyle = :dash,
        label = "California")
axislegend(ax, position = :rt, framevisible = false)
fig



Distribution of post/pre MSPE ratios across donor states (histogram). California’s ratio is the red dashed line.

title: 16  Randomization Inference for Synthetic Control
text:
16.3 Time placebo
Another check moves the treatment date backward into the pre-period. If the method finds a large placebo effect before Proposition 99, the post-treatment effect is less credible.


Code
# Pretend treatment started in 1980 instead of 1989
T0_placebo = findfirst(==(1980), years) - 1
Y_pre      = Y[:, 1:T0]   # cut off real treatment period
fit_pre    = sc_estimate(Y_pre, N0, T0_placebo)

ca_pre     = vec(Y_pre[N0 + 1, :])
ca_pre_cf  = vec(fit_pre.weights.omega' * Y_pre[1:N0, :])
placebo_effect_time = mean(ca_pre[(T0_placebo + 1):end] .- ca_pre_cf[(T0_placebo + 1):end])

@printf("Time-placebo effect (treatment moved to 1980): %.2f\n", placebo_effect_time)
@printf("Real effect (treatment in 1989):               %.2f\n", ca_effect)


Time-placebo effect (treatment moved to 1980): -3.31
Real effect (treatment in 1989):               -19.62


Here the time-placebo effect is much smaller than the real effect.
crumbs: 16  Randomization Inference for Synthetic Control

title: 16  Randomization Inference for Synthetic Control
text:
16.4 TASC posterior as Bayesian alternative
TASC models the panel with a linear Gaussian state-space process and returns a posterior distribution over the counterfactual path. This is model-based uncertainty, not a placebo distribution.


Code
Y_tasc = vcat(Y[(N0 + 1):end, :], Y[1:N0, :])
tasc_model = fit_tasc(Y_tasc; d = 2, T0 = T0, n_em = 200, tol = 1e-3)
tasc_pred  = predict_counterfactual(tasc_model, Y_tasc)

tasc_cfact = vec(tasc_pred.target)
tasc_se    = sqrt.(max.(vec(tasc_pred.variance), 0.0))
tasc_lower = tasc_cfact .- 1.96 .* tasc_se
tasc_upper = tasc_cfact .+ 1.96 .* tasc_se

# At each post-treatment year, is California outside the band?
years_post = years[(T0 + 1):end]
outside    = (ca_obs[(T0 + 1):end] .< tasc_lower[(T0 + 1):end]) .|
             (ca_obs[(T0 + 1):end] .> tasc_upper[(T0 + 1):end])
@printf("Years California is outside the 95%% band: %d/%d\n",
        sum(outside), length(outside))


Years California is outside the 95% band: 12/12




Code
# Convert placebo gaps to counterfactual paths for visualisation
fig = Figure(size = (820, 420), fontsize = 13)
ax  = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Year", ylabel = "Packs per capita",
           title = "Frequentist placebo cloud vs Bayesian posterior band")

# Placebo counterfactuals (treated outcome minus gap, mapped to California's level)
for i in 1:N0
    cf = placebo_cfacts[i, :] .+ (ca_obs[T0] - placebo_cfacts[i, T0])
    lines!(ax, years, cf, color = (:grey, 0.20), linewidth = 1)
end

band!(ax, years, tasc_lower, tasc_upper;
      color = (:seagreen, 0.25), label = "TASC 95% interval")
lines!(ax, years, ca_obs;    color = :black,     linewidth = 3, label = "California")
lines!(ax, years, ca_cfact;  color = :steelblue, linewidth = 2, label = "SC counterfactual")
lines!(ax, years, tasc_cfact; color = :seagreen,  linewidth = 2, label = "TASC counterfactual")
vlines!(ax, [years[T0] + 0.5]; color = :gray40, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 1)
axislegend(ax, position = :lb, framevisible = false)
fig



California’s observed path (black) with TASC posterior band (green), classical SC counterfactual (blue), and placebo gap envelope (grey).

The two strategies answer different questions. Randomization inference asks whether California is unusual relative to donor-state placebos. TASC asks how uncertain the model is about California’s counterfactual path. I would report both when using TASC.

title: 16  Randomization Inference for Synthetic Control
text:
16.6 Summary

With one treated unit, randomization inference is more useful than asymptotic standard errors.
Unit placebos give a reference distribution. It is design-based randomization inference only under an explicit assignment or exchangeability assumption; otherwise it is a placebo diagnostic.
MSPE ratios account for pre-treatment fit.
Time placebos check whether the method finds effects before treatment.
TASC posterior bands give model-based uncertainty for the counterfactual path, conditional on the donor pool and the state-space model. They do not price donor selection or misspecification.





Abadie, Alberto. 2021. “Using Synthetic Controls: Feasibility, Data Requirements, and Methodological Aspects.” Journal of Economic Literature 59 (2): 391–425.


Ferman, Bruno, and Cristine Pinto. 2017. “Placebo Tests for Synthetic Controls.” MPRA Paper 78079. Munich Personal RePEc Archive. https://mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de/78079/1/MPRA_paper_78079.pdf.

title: 17  IV & Regression Discontinuity
text:
17.1 Instrumental Variables
With an unobserved confounder, unconfoundedness fails. Even a randomized experiment can face this problem through noncompliance: subjects are randomly assigned but some do not comply, so the actually-treated group is self-selected and that selection may be correlated with the outcome.

title: 17  IV & Regression Discontinuity
text:
17.1.1 Uncontrolled Confounder
The graph below is the problem: \(c\) is an unobserved common cause of the treatment \(w\) and the outcome \(y\). There is no adjustment set, because \(c\) is not measured.







17.1.2 Why Does IV Work?
Adding \(z\) gives a variable that moves \(w\) and reaches \(y\) only through \(w\). The arrow \(z \to w\) is the relevance condition, and the absence of any arrow from \(z\) to \(y\) or to \(c\) is the exclusion restriction and the exogeneity condition. The missing arrows carry the assumptions.







17.1.3 IV Under Potential Outcomes

W has two potential outcomes W(1) and W(0), as a function of Z.
Y has two potential outcomes Y(1) and Y(0), as a function of W.

Intention to Treat (ITT) is the average treatment effect of the treatment assignment Z. It is the difference between the average potential outcome under treatment and the average potential outcome under control. It is the average treatment effect of the treatment assignment Z, regardless of whether the subject complies with the assignment.
There are four possible groups of subjects in the case of binary treatment and binary instrument. The groups are defined by the potential treatment status \((W(0), W(1))\) — how the subject would take treatment under each value of the instrument — not by the observed \((Z, W)\):

\(W(0)=0, W(1)=0\): never-taker
\(W(0)=0, W(1)=1\): complier
\(W(0)=1, W(1)=0\): defier
\(W(0)=1, W(1)=1\): always-taker

These four groups (strata) have different causal mechanisms. The compliers and defiers are the groups whose treatment status responds to the assignment \(Z\) — compliers in the same direction as the assignment, defiers in the opposite direction. The always-takers and never-takers take the same treatment regardless of \(Z\).
Unfortunately we cannot identify the compliance group by looking at the data.

17.1.4 Assumptions

Exclusion restriction: \(Y(w, 1) = Y(w,0)\)
Exogeneity of instrument: \(Z \perp [W(0),W(1), Y(0), Y(1)]\)
Monotonicity (no defiers): \(W(0) \leq W(1)\)



17.1.5 LATE Identification
Since we excluded defiers, and the other two groups (always-takers and never-takers) are not affected by the treatment assignment Z. The only effect we can identify is the treatment effect on the compliers. This is called the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE).
Below we write potential outcomes indexed by the instrument, \(Y(Z=z)\), rather than by treatment status, \(Y(d)\). The exclusion restriction is exactly what licenses this: since \(Y(w,1)=Y(w,0)\), \(Y\) depends on \(Z\) only through \(W\), so \(Y(Z=z) = Y(W(z), z) = Y(W(z))\) in the usual treatment-indexed notation. For a complier (\(W(1)=1, W(0)=0\)), this means \(Y(Z=1) = Y(1)\) and \(Y(Z=0) = Y(0)\), so \(E[Y(Z=1)-Y(Z=0) \mid G=C]\) below is exactly \(E[Y(1)-Y(0) \mid G=C]\), the LATE in treatment-indexed notation.
\[ \small
\begin{aligned}
& E[Y(Z=1) - Y(Z=0) | G = C] \\
&= \frac{E[Y(Z=1) - Y(Z=0)]}{P(W(1)=1, W(0)=0)} \\
&= \frac{E[Y|Z=1] - E[Y|Z=0]}{1-P(W=0|Z=1)-P(W=1|Z=0)} \text{ (monotonicity rules out D; the A and N shares subtract) } \\
&= \frac{E[Y|Z=1] - E[Y|Z=0]}{P(W=1|Z=1)-P(W=1|Z=0)} \\
&= \frac{E[Y|Z=1] - E[Y|Z=0]}{E[W|Z=1]-E[W|Z=0]}
\end{aligned}
\tag{17.1}\]


17.1.6 Parametric Models
With a binary instrument this is exactly the ratio of two OLS coefficients — no linearity assumption is needed, since a regression on a binary regressor just computes the two group means. This is sometimes called the Wald estimator.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_{LATE} &= \frac{E[Y|Z=1] - E[Y|Z=0]}{E[W|Z=1]-E[W|Z=0]} \\
&= \frac{Cov(Y,Z)}{Cov(W,Z)}
\end{aligned}
\tag{17.2}\]
Why do covariates help? It is important to separate two assumptions here. Conditioning on covariates \(X\) can make the as-if-random (conditional independence) assumption more credible: the instrument may be unconfounded only within levels of \(X\). But the exclusion restriction – that the instrument has no direct effect on the outcome – is a substantive structural assumption that covariates do not generally repair. Adding \(X\) removes a direct \(Z \to Y\) path only if that path runs entirely through \(X\), or if exclusion is conditional by design. So covariates help with conditional independence, not with exclusion per se.


17.1.7 Example
We simulate \(n = 10{,}000\) observations. Three variables \((w, m, z)\) are drawn jointly normal with mean zero and unit variances, so their covariances are also their correlations: \(\text{corr}(w,m) = 0.36\), \(\text{corr}(w,z) = 0.64\), and \(\text{corr}(m,z) = 0\). A fourth variable \(u \sim N(0,1)\) is independent of everything. The outcome is \(y = w + m + u\).
So \(m\) is the omitted confounder, correlated with the treatment \(w\) but not with the instrument \(z\), and the true coefficient on \(w\) is 1. Because all variances are 1, we can predict the omitted-variable bias exactly: regressing \(y\) on \(w\) alone gives \(1 + \text{Cov}(m,w) = 1.36\).
We fit three models: OLS of \(y\) on \(w\), OLS of \(y\) on \(w\) and \(m\), and 2SLS using \(z\) as the instrument for \(w\).


Code
## DGP: data.y = data.w + data.m + data.u
Random.seed!(66)
nobs = 10000
## here we have three variables w, m, z.
## m is the omitted variable; w and m are correlated; z is the instrument,
## which is correlated with w, but not m. u is independent of everything else.
## with unit variances, the covariances below ARE the correlations
crwm = 0.36; crmz = 0.0; crwz = 0.64
covarMat = [1.0  crwm crwz;
            crwm 1.0  crmz;
            crwz crmz 1.0]
mat  = rand(MvNormal(zeros(3), covarMat), nobs)'
data = DataFrame(w = mat[:, 1], m = mat[:, 2], z = mat[:, 3])
data.u = rand(Normal(0, 1), nobs)
# dgp
data.y = data.w .+ data.m .+ data.u
lm_biased  = feols(data, @formula(y ~ w))
lm_full    = feols(data, @formula(y ~ w + m))
tsls_model = feiv(data, @formula(y ~ 1); endo = :w, inst = :z);

display(coeftable(lm_biased))
# lm_full is good
display(coeftable(lm_full))
# tsls is good.
