OLS on \(w\) alone gives 1.3571, matching the predicted 1.36 to two decimals. OLS controlling for \(m\) gives 0.9976 on \(w\) and 0.9984 on \(m\), both close to the true 1, which is what we would do if the confounder were observed. 2SLS gives 0.9999 with a standard error of 0.0219, recovering the truth without ever using \(m\).
Note the cost of instrumenting: the 2SLS standard error is 0.0219 against 0.0107 for the OLS that controls for \(m\), twice as large. The instrument uses only the part of \(w\) that \(z\) explains, and here that is 41% of its variance.


17.1.8 Control Function Approach
Two-stage least squares can be implemented equivalently via the control function (CF) approach. Understanding why makes the extension to nonlinear models (next chapter) transparent.
Algebraic motivation. Because w is endogenous, decompose the structural error:
\[\varepsilon = \rho v + \eta, \qquad v \equiv w - E[w \mid z], \qquad E(z\eta) = 0,\; E(zv) = 0. \tag{17.3}\]
If we knew \(v\), controlling for it directly would eliminate the confounding channel. We don’t know \(v\), but the first-stage residual \(\hat v = w - \hat w\) is a consistent estimate. Substituting into the structural equation:
\[y = \alpha + \beta w + \rho\,\hat v + \text{error}. \tag{17.4}\]
OLS on this augmented second stage gives a consistent \(\hat\beta\) — identical to 2SLS by the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (FWL) theorem. The coefficient \(\hat\rho\) on \(\hat v\) doubles as a Durbin–Wu–Hausman (DWH) endogeneity test: under \(H_0\) (w is exogenous), \(\rho = 0\).


Code
import StatsBase: coef, stderror, coefnames
pick(m, v, name) = v[findfirst(==(name), coefnames(m))]

# Manual 2SLS, explicitly
stage1      = feols(data, @formula(w ~ z))
data.w_hat  = data.w .- stage1.residuals
tsls_manual = feols(data, @formula(y ~ w_hat))

# Control function: first-stage residual v_hat in the augmented regression
data.v_hat = stage1.residuals
lm_cf      = feols(data, @formula(y ~ w + v_hat))

# Compare β̂_w from manual 2SLS and CF — should be identical by FWL
@printf("Manual 2SLS   beta_w = %.8f\n", pick(tsls_manual, coef(tsls_manual), "w_hat"))
@printf("Control funct beta_w = %.8f\n", pick(lm_cf, coef(lm_cf), "w"))

# DWH endogeneity test: t-stat on v_hat
rho, rho_se = pick(lm_cf, coef(lm_cf), "v_hat"), pick(lm_cf, stderror(lm_cf), "v_hat")
@printf("DWH test on v_hat: coef = %.4f  se = %.4f  t = %.3f  p = %.4g\n",
        rho, rho_se, rho / rho_se, 2 * ccdf(Normal(), abs(rho / rho_se)))


Manual 2SLS   beta_w = 0.99987086
Control funct beta_w = 0.99987086
DWH test on v_hat: coef = 0.6100  se = 0.0270  t = 22.563  p = 9.987e-113


Both routes give \(\hat\beta_w = 0.99987086\), agreeing to all eight printed digits, which confirms FWL. The coefficient on \(\hat v\) is 0.6100 with a standard error of 0.0270, so \(t = 22.6\) and \(H_0\!:\rho = 0\) is rejected: w is endogenous. That coefficient also has a value we can derive. With \(\varepsilon = m + u\) and \(v = w - 0.64z\), we have \(\text{Cov}(\varepsilon, v) = \text{Cov}(m,w) = 0.36\) and \(\text{Var}(v) = 1 - 0.64^2 = 0.5904\), so \(\rho = 0.36/0.5904 = 0.610\). The estimate matches it to three decimals. One caveat: the OLS standard errors from the augmented regression are not valid for \(\hat\beta\) (\(\hat v\) is a generated regressor; the DWH test is fine because under \(H_0\) the first-stage estimation error does not matter). Use 2SLS standard errors, or bootstrap the two stages jointly as we do in the Poisson IV chapter.
Why FWL fails in nonlinear models. FWL is a property of linear projections; once we replace OLS with Poisson or Probit, the estimator is no longer a linear projection and the partialling-out logic does not apply. In a nonlinear second stage, \(\hat v\) must enter inside the link function (e.g. \(\exp(\mathbf{x}\boldsymbol\beta + \rho \hat v)\)), which requires a structural assumption beyond instrument exogeneity. This is the subject of the next chapter.

title: 17  IV & Regression Discontinuity
section: 17.2 When 2SLS with Covariates Is Actually LATE
text:
17.2 When 2SLS with Covariates Is Actually LATE
The LATE identification above is clean because we have no covariates. The Wald estimator gives us LATE, full stop. But in practice we usually add covariates to defend conditional exogeneity:
\[
Y = \beta W + \gamma^\top X + U, \qquad W = \pi Z + \delta^\top X + V.
\tag{17.5}\]
Does 2SLS on this still give us a LATE? Angrist and Pischke (2009) say it gives a weighted average of covariate-specific LATEs. Blandhol et al. (2025) show that this is generally not true.

17.2.1 Why the Linear Specification Hides an Assumption
By Frisch-Waugh-Lovell, the IV estimand is
\[
\beta_{iv} = \frac{E[Y \tilde Z]}{E[W \tilde Z]}, \qquad \tilde Z = Z - L[Z \mid X],
\tag{17.6}\]
where \(L[Z \mid X]\) is the linear projection of \(Z\) on \(X\). So \(\tilde Z\) is the part of \(Z\) that a linear regression on \(X\) cannot explain.
What if the true \(E[Z \mid X]\) is not linear in \(X\)? Then \(L[Z \mid X] \neq E[Z \mid X]\), and the residual instrument \(\tilde Z\) still picks up some of the conditional mean. The IV estimand then mixes treatment effects across compliance groups. Blandhol et al. (2025) prove that \(\beta_{iv}\) is a non-negatively weighted average of conditional LATEs only if the rich covariates condition holds:
\[
L[Z \mid X] = E[Z \mid X].
\tag{17.7}\]
This is a parametric assumption about \(E[Z \mid X]\). It is implicit in the linear-in-\(X\) specification, and it is rarely defended. When it fails, \(\beta_{iv}\) picks up treatment effects for always-takers as well as compliers, and some always-taker terms enter with negative weight.
“2SLS with covariates estimates LATE” is true only if \(X\) enters saturated (one dummy per cell), or the true \(E[Z \mid X]\) happens to be linear in \(X\).


17.2.2 A Simulation
We build a DGP where \(E[Z \mid X]\) is strongly nonlinear in \(X\), so the linear-in-\(X\) specification has to fail, and then compare four estimators against the true LATE.
We draw \(n = 8000\) observations with a single covariate \(X \sim U(-1,1)\). The instrument is \(Z \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_Z(X))\) with \(p_Z(X) = \Lambda(0.3 + X + 2\sin(2.5\pi X))\) — the sine term is what a linear projection cannot reproduce. Potential treatments come from one uniform draw \(U\) compared against two thresholds, \(T_0 = \mathbb{1}\{U < \Lambda(-1.6+X)\}\) and \(T_1 = \mathbb{1}\{U < \min(\Lambda(-0.4+X)+0.2,\, 0.95)\}\), so \(T_1 \ge T_0\) and monotonicity holds by construction. Observed treatment is \(W = ZT_1 + (1-Z)T_0\). The effect is heterogeneous in \(X\), \(\tau(X) = 0.5+1.5X\), and the potential outcomes are \(Y(0) = 1 + 2X + 0.8X^2 + \varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon \sim N(0,1)\) and \(Y(1) = Y(0) + \tau(X)\).
Two features matter. \(X\) enters both the instrument propensity and the treatment thresholds, so \(Z\) is exogenous only conditional on \(X\). And \(\tau\) depends on \(X\), so which units the instrument moves determines the answer.


Code
using MLJ
using DecisionTree
using Random
using Statistics
using LinearAlgebra

Random.seed!(13)
n = 8000
plogis(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z))

# Single covariate on [-1, 1]
X = 2 .* rand(n) .- 1

# True conditional mean of Z is wildly nonlinear in X.
# A linear projection L[Z|X] cannot reproduce this.
pZ_true = plogis.(0.3 .+ 1.0 .* X .+ 2.0 .* sin.(2.5 .* π .* X))
Z       = Int.(rand(n) .< pZ_true)

# Potential treatment states with monotonicity (T1 >= T0).
# X enters the propensity, so X confounds W <-> Y.
U  = rand(n)
p0 = plogis.(-1.6 .+ 1.0 .* X)
p1 = min.(plogis.(-0.4 .+ 1.0 .* X) .+ 0.2, 0.95)
T0 = Int.(U .< p0)
T1 = Int.(U .< p1)
W  = ifelse.(Z .== 1, T1, T0)

G  = [t1 == 1 && t0 == 1 ? :AT :
      t1 == 0 && t0 == 0 ? :NT : :CP
      for (t1, t0) in zip(T1, T0)]

# Heterogeneous treatment effect — varies with X
τ  = 0.5 .+ 1.5 .* X
Y0 = 1.0 .+ 2.0 .* X .+ 0.8 .* X .^ 2 .+ randn(n)
Y1 = Y0 .+ τ
Y  = ifelse.(W .== 1, Y1, Y0)

true_LATE = mean(τ[G .== :CP])
@printf("Compliance shares  AT=%.3f  CP=%.3f  NT=%.3f\n",
        mean(G .== :AT), mean(G .== :CP), mean(G .== :NT))
@printf("True unconditional LATE = %.3f\n", true_LATE)


Compliance shares  AT=0.188  CP=0.425  NT=0.388
True unconditional LATE = 0.617


The compliance shares are 18.8% always-takers, 42.5% compliers and 38.8% never-takers, and the true LATE, the mean of \(\tau\) over compliers, is 0.617.
We now compare four estimators against it: the unconditional Wald ratio, 2SLS with \(X\) entered linearly, 2SLS with a degree-7 polynomial in \(X\), and DDML PLIV with random-forest nuisance learners. Julia has no counterpart of R’s DoubleML package, so we write the PLIV cross-fitting out.


Code
# Helper: TSLS via the matrix expression (Xmat is the exogenous matrix incl.
# constant). Returns the coefficient on W and its conventional standard error.
function tsls_matrix(Y, W, Z, Xmat)
    Wmat = hcat(W, Xmat)
    Zmat = hcat(Z, Xmat)
    What = Zmat * ((Zmat' * Zmat) \ (Zmat' * Wmat))
    β    = (What' * Wmat) \ (What' * Y)
    e    = Y .- Wmat * β
    σ2   = sum(abs2, e) / (length(Y) - size(Wmat, 2))
    return β[1], sqrt(σ2 * inv(What' * What)[1, 1])
end

# (a) Wald — biased: Z is not unconditionally exogenous because X confounds.
wald = (mean(Y[Z .== 1]) - mean(Y[Z .== 0])) /
       (mean(W[Z .== 1]) - mean(W[Z .== 0]))

# (b) TSLS with X entered linearly — the textbook spec.
b_lin, se_lin = tsls_matrix(Float64.(Y), Float64.(W), Float64.(Z), hcat(ones(n), X))

# (c) TSLS with a rich basis (polynomial up to degree 7) — closer to saturation.
b_poly, se_poly = tsls_matrix(Float64.(Y), Float64.(W), Float64.(Z),
                              hcat([X .^ k for k in 0:7]...))

# (d) DDML PLIV with random-forest nuisance learners and 5-fold cross-fitting.
RandomForestRegressor = @load RandomForestRegressor pkg=DecisionTree verbosity=0
learner = RandomForestRegressor(n_trees = 500, max_depth = 5)

nsplits = 5
s       = shuffle(1:n)
folds   = [s[1 + floor(Int, (k-1)*n/nsplits) : floor(Int, k*n/nsplits)]
           for k in 1:nsplits]

mY = zeros(n); mW = zeros(n); mZ = zeros(n)
Xtab = DataFrame(X = X)
for fold_idx in 1:nsplits
    test  = folds[fold_idx]
    train = setdiff(1:n, test)
    for (out, dest) in ((Y, mY), (W, mW), (Z, mZ))
        mach = machine(learner, Xtab[train, :], Float64.(out[train]))
        MLJ.fit!(mach, verbosity = 0)
        dest[test] = MLJ.predict(mach, Xtab[test, :])
    end
end

rY = Y .- mY; rW = W .- mW; rZ = Z .- mZ
b_pliv  = sum(rZ .* rY) / sum(rZ .* rW)
ψ       = (rY .- b_pliv .* rW) .* rZ              # PLIV score
se_pliv = sqrt(mean(ψ .^ 2) / mean(rW .* rZ)^2 / n)

results = DataFrame(
    Estimator = ["True LATE",
                 "Wald (no covariates)",
                 "TSLS, X linear",
                 "TSLS, poly(X, 7)",
                 "DDML PLIV (cross-fit, random forest)"],
    Estimate  = round.([true_LATE, wald, b_lin, b_poly, b_pliv], digits = 3),
    SE        = [missing, missing, round(se_lin, digits = 3), round(se_poly, digits = 3),
                 round(se_pliv, digits = 3)]
)

The linear-in-\(X\) 2SLS does not recover the true LATE — and neither do the more flexible versions. Two things are going on, and the standard errors in the table help separate them. First, the estimands differ: for this DGP the linear-projection 2SLS converges to 0.55, and the polynomial 2SLS and DDML PLIV converge to approximately \(\beta_{rich} = 0.58\) (computable by integrating the weight formula below), all below the LATE of 0.617 — a real but modest gap that persists at any sample size. Second, sampling noise: the SEs are 0.06 to 0.07, and in this draw each estimate lands within 0.01 of its own estimand, at 0.552, 0.585 and 0.582, so here the whole gap to the LATE is the difference in estimands. The Wald estimator is far off for a different reason entirely, at 1.910 against a truth of 0.617: \(Z\) is not unconditionally exogenous, and Wald has no way to use \(X\).
What are the polynomial 2SLS and DDML PLIV estimating, if not LATE? PLIV targets \(\beta_{rich}\), a weighted average of conditional LATEs with weights proportional to \(\text{Var}(Z \mid X) \cdot P(\text{complier} \mid X)\); the polynomial 2SLS targets nearly the same quantity (a degree-7 polynomial cannot fully reproduce this \(E[Z \mid X]\), so its estimand is a misspecified-projection variant sitting just below \(\beta_{rich}\)). These are non-negatively weighted, so weakly causal. But they are not the unconditional LATE we usually want.


17.2.3 Diagnostic: RESET on Z ~ X
Rich covariates says \(E[Z \mid X]\) is linear in \(X\). That is exactly the null of Ramsey’s RESET test (Ramsey 1969). We can apply it to a regression of \(Z\) on \(X\) and see whether higher-order terms of \(X\) are jointly significant.


Code
using GLM
# RESET with type = "regressor", power = 2:3: F-test of X^2 and X^3 added to Z ~ X
df_reset       = DataFrame(Z = Float64.(Z), X = X, X2 = X .^ 2, X3 = X .^ 3)
m_restricted   = lm(@formula(Z ~ X), df_reset)
m_unrestricted = lm(@formula(Z ~ X + X2 + X3), df_reset)
rss_r, rss_u   = sum(abs2, residuals(m_restricted)), sum(abs2, residuals(m_unrestricted))
q, k_u         = 2, 4
F_stat         = ((rss_r - rss_u) / q) / (rss_u / (n - k_u))
@printf("RESET = %.2f, df1 = %d, df2 = %d, p-value = %.3g\n",
        F_stat, q, n - k_u, ccdf(FDist(q, n - k_u), F_stat))


RESET = 131.57, df1 = 2, df2 = 7996, p-value = 6.03e-57


It rejects strongly here, \(\text{RESET} = 131.6\) on 2 and 7,996 degrees of freedom with \(p < 10^{-56}\), which is the right answer given that we put a sine wave in \(E[Z \mid X]\). The same test on real data is cheap, and it tells us whether the LATE interpretation is defensible before we report a 2SLS coefficient.


17.2.4 What to Do Instead
Blandhol et al. (2025) give four steps for empirical work.

Reconsider the covariates. If \(Z\) is unconditionally exogenous, drop them. A kitchen-sink set of controls makes rich covariates less likely.
Run RESET on Z ~ X. If it does not reject, the linear-IV-as-LATE interpretation is defensible.
If RESET rejects, report DDML PLIV alongside 2SLS. That is what the cross-fitting chunk above does. DDML PLIV targets \(\beta_{rich}\), a non-negatively weighted average of conditional LATEs.
For a binary instrument, also estimate the unconditional LATE. With instrument propensity score weighting (Słoczyński 2024),
\[
\hat\beta_{late} = \frac{\sum_i Y_i [Z_i/\hat p(X_i) - (1-Z_i)/(1-\hat p(X_i))]}{\sum_i W_i [Z_i/\hat p(X_i) - (1-Z_i)/(1-\hat p(X_i))]},
\tag{17.8}\]
where \(\hat p(X) = P(Z = 1 \mid X)\) is estimated nonparametrically. Stata has kappalate (Słoczyński, Uysal and Wooldridge), which implements this and related weighting estimators of the LATE. In Julia it is straightforward to build once \(\hat p(X)\) is in hand.



17.2.5 A Note on the FRDD Example
The fuzzy-RDD example at the end of this chapter is 2SLS with race, state of birth, and quarter-of-birth fixed effects entered as covariates. That section traces the gap between the 2SLS and the local rdrobust estimates to the first stage, which is close to zero near the cutoff. Rich covariates is a separate question about the 2SLS estimate itself, and the RESET test on the above-cutoff instrument against those covariates is the right first thing to run.


17.2.6 Bottom Line
“2SLS with covariates estimates LATE” needs the rich covariates condition. That condition is a parametric assumption on \(E[Z \mid X]\) that researchers rarely defend, and a simple RESET test often rejects it. The honest alternatives are DDML PLIV for \(\beta_{rich}\) and IPSW (or DDML) for the unconditional LATE. Even when rich covariates holds, \(\beta_{rich}\) can be quite different from the unconditional LATE we usually care about.

title: 17  IV & Regression Discontinuity
text:
17.3 Regression Discontinuity Design
RDD (regression discontinuity design) is a quasi-experimental design that is used to estimate causal effects of interventions when assignment to the intervention is determined by whether a subject’s value on an observed covariate exceeds a threshold. The idea is that the assignment is as good as random, so we can estimate the causal effect of the intervention by comparing the outcomes of subjects who are just above and just below the threshold.

17.3.1 Sharp RDD
We have a continuous variable \(X\), called the running variable, which determines the binary treatment \(W\). The treatment is assigned according to a threshold \(c\). The outcome variable \(Y\) is a function of \(X\) and \(W\).
\[ W=\mathbb{1}(X>c) \tag{17.9}\]
Lee (2008) studies the effect of incumbency advantage in elections. His identification strategy is based on the discontinuity generated by the rule that the party with a majority vote share wins. The forcing variable \(X_i\) is the difference in vote share between the Democratic and Republican parties in one election, with the threshold \(c = 0\). The outcome variable \(Y_i\) is vote share at the second election.
rdplot bins the running variable and returns bin means and a polynomial fit on each side of the cutoff, which we plot. A visible jump at zero is the design working.


Code
senate = CSV.read("data/rdrobust_senate.csv", DataFrame)

# Calculate RD plot data
plot_data = rdplot(senate.vote, senate.margin, c=0.0)

fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel="Margin", ylabel="Vote")
scatter!(ax, plot_data.vars_bins.rdplot_mean_x, plot_data.vars_bins.rdplot_mean_y, 
         color=:gray, markersize=6)

# Plot polynomial fit for left side
poly_l = filter(r -> r.rdplot_x < 0.0, plot_data.vars_poly)
lines!(ax, poly_l.rdplot_x, poly_l.rdplot_y, color=:blue, linewidth=2)

# Plot polynomial fit for right side
poly_r = filter(r -> r.rdplot_x >= 0.0, plot_data.vars_poly)
lines!(ax, poly_r.rdplot_x, poly_r.rdplot_y, color=:blue, linewidth=2)

vlines!(ax, [0.0], color=:black, linestyle=:dash)
fig





The rdrobust_RDsenate data are 1,297 US Senate races. The running variable margin is the Democratic margin of victory in an election and vote is the Democratic vote share in the next election for the same seat. The bin means step up discontinuously at a margin of zero.


17.3.2 Identification of SRDD
\[ \tau_{RD} = \lim_{x \to c^+} E[Y|X=x] - \lim_{x \to c^-} E[Y|X=x]  \tag{17.10}\]
In words, the treatment effect is the difference in the outcome from the right side and from the left side. This is the same as the difference in the outcome at the threshold, as if the treatment is assigned randomly.


17.3.3 Estimation of SRDD
Before the real data, a simulation where we know the answer. We draw \(n = 1000\) students with \(\text{GPA} \sim U(0,4)\) and outcome \(Y = 10 + 1.5\,\text{GPA} + 2 \cdot \mathbb{1}\{\text{GPA} > 3\} + \varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon \sim N(0,1)\). The cutoff is 3 and the true jump is 2. The running variable also has a direct effect on the outcome, with slope 1.5, which is what the local regression on each side has to absorb.


Code
Random.seed!(2024)
GPA = rand(Uniform(0, 4), 1000)
# Treatment is W = 1(GPA > 3), so the +2 jump must sit on the right
# (above-cutoff) side to match the right-minus-left estimand above.
future_success = 10 .+ 1.5 .* GPA .+ 2 .* (GPA .> 3) .+ rand(Normal(0, 1), 1000)

plot_data_gpa = rdplot(future_success, GPA, c = 3.0)

fig2 = Figure()
ax2 = Axis(fig2[1, 1], xlabel = "GPA", ylabel = "Future Success")
scatter!(ax2, plot_data_gpa.vars_bins.rdplot_mean_x, plot_data_gpa.vars_bins.rdplot_mean_y,
         color = :gray, markersize = 6)
poly_gpa_l = filter(r -> r.rdplot_x < 3.0, plot_data_gpa.vars_poly)
lines!(ax2, poly_gpa_l.rdplot_x, poly_gpa_l.rdplot_y, color = :blue, linewidth = 2)
poly_gpa_r = filter(r -> r.rdplot_x >= 3.0, plot_data_gpa.vars_poly)
lines!(ax2, poly_gpa_r.rdplot_x, poly_gpa_r.rdplot_y, color = :blue, linewidth = 2)
vlines!(ax2, [3.0], color = :black, linestyle = :dash)
fig2







Code
# a compact summary, like R's summary() of an rdrobust fit
function rd_summary(r)
    @printf("Bandwidth h = %.3f, b = %.3f; N = %d left, %d right; effective N = %d left, %d right\n",
            r.bws.h_left[1], r.bws.b_left[1], r.N[1], r.N[2], r.N_h[1], r.N_h[2])
    DataFrame(Method = r.coef.Method, Coef = round.(r.coef.Coeff, digits = 4),
              SE = round.(r.se.StdErr, digits = 4), p = round.(r.pv.PValue, sigdigits = 3),
              CI_low = round.(r.ci.CILower, digits = 3), CI_high = round.(r.ci.CIUpper, digits = 3))
end

# estimate the sharp RDD model
rdd_gpa = rdrobust(future_success, GPA, c = 3.0)
rd_summary(rdd_gpa)

17.3.5 Fuzzy RDD
In fuzzy RDD, the treatment is assigned according to a threshold \(c\), but there exist non-compliance. This is similar to IV case.
\[ \tau_{FRD} = \frac{\lim_{x \to c^+} E[Y|X=x] - \lim_{x \to c^-} E[Y|X=x]}{\lim_{x \to c^+} E[W|X=x] - \lim_{x \to c^-} E[W|X=x]}  \tag{17.11}\]
For example, if food stamp eligibility is given to all households below a certain income, but not all households receive the food stamps. In other words, income does not solely determine the assignment. Cutoff point increases the probability of treatment but doesn’t completely determine treatment.
FRDD is IV.


17.3.6 FRDD Example
Fetter (2013)’s main question of interest is how much of the increase in the home ownership rate in the midcentury US was due to mortgage subsidies given out by the government.
We’re using the running variable quarter of birth (qob), which has been centered on the quarter of birth you’d need to be to be eligible for a mortgage subsidy for fighting in the Korean War (qob_minus_kw). This determines whether you were a veteran of either the Korean War or World War II (vet_wwko).


Code
vet = CSV.read("data/mortgages.csv", DataFrame)   # causaldata::mortgages
# Create an "above-cutoff" variable as the instrument
vet.above = Float64.(vet.qob_minus_kw .> 0)
# Impose a bandwidth of 12 quarters on either side
vet = vet[abs.(vet.qob_minus_kw) .< 12, :]
# The running variable qob_minus_kw is exogenous, so it goes with the controls.
# The endogenous regressors are veteran status and its interaction with the
# running variable, instrumented by being above the cutoff and that interaction.
vet.vet_inter   = vet.qob_minus_kw .* vet.vet_wwko
vet.above_inter = vet.qob_minus_kw .* vet.above
m = feiv(vet, @formula(home_ownership ~ nonwhite + qob_minus_kw + fe(bpl) + fe(qob));
         endo = [:vet_wwko, :vet_inter], inst = [:above, :above_inter],
         vcov_type = Vcov.robust())   # heteroskedasticity-robust SEs

Now the same design estimated locally with rdrobust. We pass race and state of birth as covariates, but not quarter of birth. Quarter of birth is a function of the running variable, and the local window holds only three quarters on each side of the cutoff. There the quarter-of-birth dummies duplicate the local linear fits, and the jump is not identified with them in. rdrobust still returns a number, but the number is arbitrary: with the dummies included, R’s rdrobust gives 0.096 or 0.838, depending only on whether the covariate matrix carries an intercept column. title: 17  IV & Regression Discontinuity
text:
17.4 Summary
An instrument recovers an effect when the confounder is unobserved. It must move the treatment (relevance), reach the outcome only through the treatment (exclusion) and be as good as random. With heterogeneous effects and no defiers, the Wald ratio identifies the LATE, the effect on compliers. Adding covariates linearly keeps that interpretation only under the rich-covariates condition, that the instrument’s conditional mean is linear in the covariates. A RESET test on the instrument checks it. Regression discontinuity replaces the instrument with a cutoff in a running variable and assumes continuity at the cutoff. Fuzzy RDD is IV at the cutoff.
In the simulation, OLS gives 1.3571, and 2SLS gives 0.9999 against a true 1. With a nonlinear instrument propensity, the true LATE is 0.617 and the linear 2SLS converges to 0.55. The Senate incumbency effect is 7.4 percentage points. In the Korean War example, 2SLS gives 0.1702 (0.0459). The local rdrobust estimate, 2.37 (4.97), is uninformative, because veteran status does not jump at the cutoff within the local window. The 2SLS first stage comes from linear fits over 12 quarters.




Angrist, Joshua D., and Jörn-Steffen Pischke. 2009. Mostly Harmless Econometrics: An Empiricist’s Companion. Princeton University Press.


Blandhol, Christine, John Bonney, Magne Mogstad, and Alexander Torgovitsky. 2025. “When Is TSLS Actually LATE?”


Ramsey, J. B. 1969. “Tests for Specification Errors in Classical Linear Least-Squares Regression Analysis.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 31 (2): 350–71.


Słoczyński, Tymon. 2024. “When Should We (Not) Interpret Linear IV Estimands as LATE?” Quantitative Economics.

title: 18  Shift-Share Instrumental Variables
text:
18.1 The construction
Shift-share, or Bartik, instruments answer one specific problem, so it is clearest to write the regression down first.
We want the effect of a local economic shock on a local outcome. For region \(\ell\),
\[
Y_\ell \;=\; \beta X_\ell + Z_\ell'\gamma + u_\ell ,
\tag{18.1}\]
where \(X_\ell\) is the shock the region actually experienced — local import competition per worker, in the China-shock literature — and \(Y_\ell\) is the outcome, say the change in the local manufacturing employment share. The parameter we want is \(\beta\).
The endogenous regressor is \(X_\ell\). Regions do not receive their shocks at random. A region whose import competition rises sharply may be a region whose industries were already losing ground, and whatever caused that decline sits in \(u_\ell\) and moves \(Y_\ell\) on its own. Then \(\text{Cov}(X_\ell, u_\ell) \ne 0\), and OLS mixes the effect of the shock with the local conditions that produced it. We cannot sign that bias in advance; it depends on whether those local conditions push the outcome up or down.
The shift-share instrument replaces the realised local shock with a predicted one, assembled from two pieces that are meant to have nothing to do with \(u_\ell\): each region’s baseline industry shares, fixed before the outcome period, and national or foreign industry-level shocks, common across regions. A region with a large baseline share in an industry is mechanically more exposed to a shock hitting that industry, and that exposure is predicted rather than realised.
Building the instrument is the easy part. The difficult part is saying which of the two pieces carries the exogeneity assumption — the shares, the shocks, or both — because the two answers lead to different identification arguments, different diagnostics, and different standard errors. That is what the rest of the chapter is about.
For each location \(\ell\) and industry \(k\), let \(s_{\ell k}\) be the share of local employment in industry \(k\) at baseline, and let \(g_k\) be a national growth rate (or trade shock) for that industry. The shift-share instrument is
\[
B_\ell \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} s_{\ell k}\, g_k.
\tag{18.2}\]
This is “shift-share” because it combines a local share with an industry-level shift. Bartik (1991) used local industry mix to predict local employment growth. Autor, Dorn, and Hanson (2013) used local industry shares interacted with industry-level Chinese import growth in other high-income countries.
The first-stage regression is then
\[
\Delta L_\ell \;=\; \pi_0 + \pi_1 B_\ell + X_\ell'\gamma + \epsilon_\ell,
\tag{18.3}\]
with \(B_\ell\) instrumenting for the observed local shock in a 2SLS for the outcome of interest.

title: 18  Shift-Share Instrumental Variables
text:
18.2 Two identification views
There are two ways to justify a shift-share instrument. They put the exogeneity assumption on different objects.

18.2.1 Share view (GPSS 2020)
Treat the shares \(s_{\ell k}\) as the source of identifying variation, with the shocks \(g_k\) acting as weights. The instrument is valid if shares are exogenous to the outcome (conditional on controls). GPSS prove that the shift-share IV is numerically equivalent to a GMM combination of \(K\) just-identified IVs, one per industry share:
\[
\hat\beta^{SS} \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat\alpha_k\, \hat\beta_k,
\tag{18.4}\]
where \(\hat\beta_k\) is the just-identified IV using share \(s_{\cdot k}\) alone and \(\hat\alpha_k\) is the Rotemberg weight. This gives an important diagnostic: which industry shares are driving the estimate?


18.2.2 Shock view (BHJ 2022)
Treat the shocks \(g_k\) as the source of identifying variation. Shares are exposure weights. Under this view, shocks should be uncorrelated with the second-stage unobservables, conditional on industry-level controls. BHJ show how to rewrite the regression at the shock level.
The two views are not mutually exclusive. In an application, we should be clear which one is being defended and report diagnostics for both.

title: 18  Shift-Share Instrumental Variables
text:
18.3 Inference
Standard OLS or cluster-robust standard errors on the regional regression underestimate uncertainty because the same industry shocks appear in many regions, inducing cross-region correlation that region-level clustering does not capture. Two corrections are now standard:

Cluster on shocks (BHJ): equivalent to running the regression at the industry-shock level. Implemented via the bhj_collapse function.
AKM SE (Adão, Kolesár, Morales 2019): explicit formula accounting for shock-level correlation; requires custom implementation or a dedicated package.

14            0.270    0.003   -0.013
15            0.631    0.003   -3.240
16            2.271    0.204    0.746

19            0.020   -0.000    1.234

GPSS identity: Σ α_k β_k = 0.5309
Shift-share IV estimate: 0.5309


Two diagnostics matter:

Weight concentration: if one or two industries carry most of the weight, the identifying variation is essentially coming from those industries’ shares. Their exogeneity is the assumption you are really leaning on.
Heterogeneous \(\hat\beta_k\): in this benign simulation, the industry-specific IVs are all near the true effect (with sampling noise). In real data, if a few industries give wildly different estimates, the “average” shift-share IV is averaging over heterogeneous treatment effects you should report explicitly.



Code
fig = Figure(size = (640, 380))
ax  = Axis(fig[1, 1],
           xlabel = "Industry",
           ylabel = "Just-identified IV estimate (β_k)",
           title  = "Industry-level IV estimates and Rotemberg weights")

# Bubble plot: position = beta_k, size = |alpha_k|
scatter!(ax, rw.industry, rw.beta_k,
         markersize = 30 .* sqrt.(abs.(rw.alpha)),
         color = (:steelblue, 0.7))
hlines!(ax, [beta_true], color = :firebrick, linestyle = :dash,
        linewidth = 2, label = "True β = $(beta_true)")
axislegend(ax, position = :rb, framevisible = false)
fig







18.4.2 What goes wrong when shares are endogenous
Now break the share-exogeneity assumption: make industry 1’s share correlated with the second-stage error.


Code
v = CSV.read("data/shift_share_bad_v.csv", DataFrame).v
shares_bad = copy(shares)
shares_bad[:, 1] .= max.(0.01, shares[:, 1] .+ 0.15 .* v)
shares_bad = shares_bad ./ sum(shares_bad, dims=2)   # renormalise

bad_noise = CSV.read("data/shift_share_bad_noise.csv", DataFrame)
B_bad = bartik_iv(shares_bad, shocks)
X_bad = B_bad .+ 0.3 .* u .+ bad_noise.noise_x
Y_bad = beta_true .* X_bad .+ u .+ 0.6 .* v .+ bad_noise.noise_y

df_bad  = DataFrame(X = X_bad, Y = Y_bad, B = B_bad)
iv_bad  = feiv(df_bad, @formula(Y ~ 1), endo = :X, inst = :B)

@printf("True beta: %.3f\n", beta_true)
@printf("Shift-share IV with bad share 1: %.3f\n", coef(iv_bad)[1])

# Would the Rotemberg weights have flagged industry 1?
rw_bad = rotemberg_weights(shares_bad, shocks, X_bad, Y_bad)
ord    = sortperm(abs.(rw_bad.alpha), rev = true)
rank1  = findfirst(==(1), rw_bad.industry[ord])
@printf("Rotemberg weight of industry 1: %.3f (rank %d of %d by |α|)\n",
        rw_bad.alpha[rw_bad.industry .== 1][1], rank1, nrow(rw_bad))

# Leave-one-industry-out: rebuild the instrument without industry 1
B_loo  = bartik_iv(shares_bad[:, 2:end], shocks[2:end])
df_loo = DataFrame(X = X_bad, Y = Y_bad, B = B_loo)
iv_loo = feiv(df_loo, @formula(Y ~ 1), endo = :X, inst = :B)
@printf("Leave-industry-1-out IV: %.3f\n", coef(iv_loo)[1])


True beta: 0.500
Shift-share IV with bad share 1: 0.798
Rotemberg weight of industry 1: 0.110 (rank 3 of 20 by |α|)
Leave-industry-1-out IV: 0.480


The estimate is biased, and the bias comes from one industry’s share being related to the error. Note what the diagnostics do and do not catch here. The endogenous industry’s Rotemberg weight is unremarkable — it ranks third of twenty — because the weights measure influence (whose exogeneity the estimate leans on most), not endogeneity. An industry with a modest weight can still move the estimate substantially when its share is correlated with the error. What isolates the problem is the leave-one-industry-out check: dropping industry 1 from the instrument restores an estimate close to the truth.

title: 18  Shift-Share Instrumental Variables
text:
18.5 BHJ shock-level inference
Collapse the location-level data to the shock level and run a weighted IV at the shock (industry) level. This reframes the identifying assumption: shocks must be uncorrelated with the shock-level aggregated outcome residual.


Code
collapsed = bhj_collapse(shares, shocks, Y, X)

# BHJ shock-level 2SLS: regress Y_agg ~ X_agg | shock, weighted by weight
df_collapsed = collapsed
iv_bhj = feiv(df_collapsed, @formula(Y_agg ~ 1),
              endo = :X_agg, inst = :shock, weights = :weight)

@printf("Location-level shift-share IV: %.3f\n", coef(ivss)[1])
@printf("BHJ shock-level IV:             %.3f\n", coef(iv_bhj)[1])
@printf("(Identical in the no-controls case)\n")


Location-level shift-share IV: 0.531
BHJ shock-level IV:             0.531
(Identical in the no-controls case)


The BHJ shock-level regression gives exactly the location-level IV estimate when there are no controls. Its value is interpretive: validity is now a statement about shocks (20 observations, one per industry) rather than locations (500 observations), and testing shock-level exogeneity is more transparent.

title: 18  Shift-Share Instrumental Variables
section: 18.6 Empirical: the China shock (Autor, Dorn, Hanson 2013)
text:
18.6 Empirical: the China shock (Autor, Dorn, Hanson 2013)
The standard shift-share application is ADH (2013). Commuting zones are exposed differently to Chinese import competition because their baseline industry mixes differ. The instrument is
\[
\text{IV}_\ell \;=\; \sum_k \frac{L_{\ell k,\,1990}}{L_{\ell,\,1990}}\,
                   \frac{\Delta M^{\text{other}}_{k}}{L_{k,\,1990}},
\tag{18.5}\]
where the shocks \(\Delta M^{\text{other}}_k\) are growth in Chinese imports into other high-income countries. This leave-one-out construction removes US-specific demand from the shock.
The snippet below is schematic — the full ADH specification additionally needs period effects, the ADH control set, and population weights (a validated replication against the GPSS benchmark lives in the ShiftShareIV.jl repository).


Code
# David Dorn distributes the replication data at ddorn.net
# Files needed:
#   workfile_china.csv  (commuting zone data, 1990–2007)
#   industry_shares.csv (czone × industry shares)

using CSV
cz     = DataFrame(CSV.File("data/workfile_china.csv"))
shares = Matrix(select(cz, r"share_"))   # L × K share matrix
shocks = cz.import_shock_other            # K-vector of "other-countries" shocks

B   = bartik_iv(shares, shocks)               # Bartik instrument
df_adh = hcat(cz, DataFrame(B = B))

# First-stage + second-stage
iv_adh = feiv(df_adh, @formula(d_sh_empl_mfg ~ 1),
              endo = :d_tradeusch_pw, inst = :B,
              vcov_type = Vcov.cluster(:statefip))

# Rotemberg decomposition
rw_adh = rotemberg_weights(shares, shocks, df_adh.d_tradeusch_pw,
                           df_adh.d_sh_empl_mfg)
# Top 5 industries by |alpha|:
sort(rw_adh, :alpha, rev=true)[1:5, :]

# BHJ shock-level regression
collapsed_adh = bhj_collapse(shares, shocks, df_adh.d_sh_empl_mfg,
                             df_adh.d_tradeusch_pw)
iv_bhj_adh = feiv(collapsed_adh, @formula(Y_agg ~ 1),
                  endo = :X_agg, inst = :shock, weights = :weight)


For a new shift-share paper, I would expect:

Rotemberg weights (via rotemberg_weights): identify which industries drive the estimate; flag weight concentration and heterogeneous \(\hat\beta_k\).
BHJ shock-level regression (via bhj_collapse): reframe validity as a statement about 20 industry shocks rather than 500 commuting zones.
AKM standard errors (Adão, Kolesár, Morales 2019): account for shock-level correlation in inference. Requires custom implementation; see the accompanying R chapter for an R-based version.

title: 18  Shift-Share Instrumental Variables
text:
18.7 Summary

Shift-share IV combines local shares and industry shocks.
The GPSS view puts exogeneity on shares; the BHJ view puts it on shocks.
Rotemberg weights show which industry shares drive the 2SLS estimate.
Region-level clustering is usually too optimistic. Use shock-level inference and AKM standard errors when possible.
ShiftShareIV.jl provides bartik_iv, rotemberg_weights, and bhj_collapse; Panelest.jl provides feols and feiv.

title: 19  Recentered Formula Instruments
text:
19.1 Formula instruments
Many treatments are computed from a formula that combines a random shock with non-random exposure. Medicaid eligibility is a state’s rules applied to a person’s income. Import exposure is national industry shocks applied to a region’s industry mix. The Bartik instrument of the previous chapter is one such formula. This chapter covers the general version of Borusyak and Hull (Borusyak and Hull 2023), their result on which formula is best (Borusyak and Hull 2026), and what both mean for shift-share.
Unit \(i\) has outcome \(y_i\) and treatment \(x_i\), with a constant effect \(\beta\):
\[
y_i = \beta x_i + \varepsilon_i .
\tag{19.1}\]
The treatment is \(x_i = h_i(g, w, u)\), where \(h_i\) is a known function, \(g\) collects the random shocks, \(w\) collects predetermined variables such as income or industry shares, and \(u\) collects anything else. The identifying assumption puts all the randomness on the shocks (Borusyak and Hull 2026, Assumption 1):
\[
E[\varepsilon_i \mid g, w] = E[\varepsilon_i \mid w] .
\tag{19.2}\]
The error may depend on \(w\) in any way. Poorer people may have worse outcomes, and regions with more manufacturing may have been declining anyway.
A formula instrument is \(z_i = f_i(g, w)\) for a fixed function \(f_i\). Its expected value over the shock draws, holding \(w\) fixed, is the expected instrument \(\mu_i = E[z_i \mid w]\). The recentered instrument \(\tilde z_i = z_i - \mu_i\) is valid, because by iterated expectations and Equation 19.2,
\[
E[\tilde z_i \varepsilon_i]
= E\big[\tilde z_i\, E[\varepsilon_i \mid w]\big]
= E\big[E[\tilde z_i \mid w]\, E[\varepsilon_i \mid w]\big] = 0 .
\]
Without recentering the same steps give \(E[z_i \varepsilon_i] = E[\mu_i
E[\varepsilon_i \mid w]]\), which is not zero when the expected instrument is correlated with the predictable part of the error. Subtracting \(\mu_i\) and controlling for \(\mu_i\) are equivalent by Frisch–Waugh–Lovell. Computing \(\mu_i\) requires the design: how the shocks could have been drawn. We redraw them from that design, or permute them if they are exchangeable, and average the formula over the draws.
Any recentered formula is valid, so we can pick the most precise. Borusyak and Hull (2026, Theorem 1) show it starts from the best prediction of the treatment, recentered:
\[
\tilde z = E[x \mid g, w] - E[x \mid w] .
\tag{19.3}\]
The full optimal instrument adds two refinements, partly controlling for the predictable part of the error and GLS weighting, which need a model of the error. The authors drop them. Their algorithm predicts the treatment from its formula, recenters the prediction by redrawing the shocks, and uses the result as the instrument. When \(x_i\) depends only on \((g, w)\), the prediction is \(x_i\) itself.

title: 19  Recentered Formula Instruments
text:
19.2 Shift-share as a formula instrument
The Bartik instrument \(B_\ell = \sum_k s_{\ell k} g_k\) of Equation 18.2 is the linear formula, shares times shocks. It differs from Equation 19.3 in two ways.
The first is recentering. Suppose the industry shocks are exchangeable within period \(t\), with mean \(\bar g_t\), and let \(S_\ell = \sum_k s_{\ell k}\) be region \(\ell\)’s sum of shares. Then
\[
\mu_\ell = S_\ell\, \bar g_t .
\tag{19.4}\]
If the shares sum to one, \(\mu_\ell = \bar g_t\) is common to all regions and period effects absorb it, so Bartik is already recentered. If they are incomplete, as with manufacturing shares, heavily manufacturing regions get a large instrument in every draw, and Bartik is biased unless we control for \(S_\ell\) interacted with period (Borusyak, Hull, and Jaravel 2022).
The second is the formula. Take two regions with half their employment in electronics, and an import shock to electronics. Region A’s plants compete with Chinese imports. Region B’s make military components and do not. Bartik gives both half the shock, but only A’s import competition rises, so the instrument varies where the treatment does not. The best predictor gives A half the shock and B nothing, then recenters each by its own expected value. Both instruments are valid, and the second has the stronger first stage. When the treatment really is shares times shocks, the best predictor is Bartik itself and the two differ only by recentering. The formula matters when the treatment has more structure than Bartik uses: eligibility rules, export exposure, transport networks, nonlinear indices.



Table 19.1: Shift-share and recentered formula instruments.











Shift-share (Bartik)

The formula instrument needs more inputs: the treatment’s formula and an explicit shock design. With heterogeneous effects, different instruments weight units differently, so a gain in precision is a gain for a different weighted average (Borusyak and Hull 2026, Proposition D1).

19.2.1 Why recenter
Bartik needs one of two assumptions. If the shares are as good as random given the controls (Goldsmith-Pinkham, Sorkin, and Swift 2020), Bartik is valid as it stands and recentering is not needed. If only the shocks are random (Borusyak, Hull, and Jaravel 2022), the shares may be correlated with the error. Writing each shock as the mean shock plus a deviation splits the instrument in two:
\[
B_\ell = S_\ell\, \bar g_t + \sum_k s_{\ell k}\,(g_k - \bar g_t) .
\tag{19.5}\]
The first part is the expected instrument of Equation 19.4. It depends only on how much exposure the region has, so with incomplete shares a region with more exposure gets a larger value in every draw, and this part is correlated with the error whenever exposure is. The second part depends on whether the region’s industries received larger or smaller shocks than average. If the shocks are independent of the shares and the errors, the deviations average to zero whatever the shares are, so this part is uncorrelated with the error. Recentering keeps only the second part. When the shares sum to one, the first part is \(\bar g_t\) for every region and the period effects absorb it.
This gives the formula instrument four advantages. Its validity rests only on the shocks, such as a policy choice or a foreign supply shock, which are often easier to defend than the shares. The design has to be written down, so the assumption is explicit and can be varied, as the two ADH designs below show. The instrument can use exposure to gain power, because the best predictor tracks the treatment more closely than a shock-only index. And it is not tied to a linear formula or to independent units: it covers eligibility rules, networks and nonlinear indices, with shocks shared by many units.

title: 19  Recentered Formula Instruments
text:
19.3 Simulation
The aim is to compare a shock-only instrument with the recentered treatment when we know the true effect. There are 50 states and 10,000 people. Person \(i\) lives in state \(s(i)\) and has income \(\text{inc}_i\), in multiples of the poverty line, drawn from a log-normal distribution with median 1.4. The shock is the states’ policy: each state \(k\) draws an eligibility threshold \(T_k\) from \(\{0.5, 1, 1.38, 2\}\), each value with probability 1/4, independently across states. Eligibility and the outcome are
\[
x_i = 1[\text{inc}_i < T_{s(i)}], \qquad
y_i = 0.3\, x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad
\varepsilon_i = -0.5 \log \text{inc}_i + \alpha_{s(i)} + \nu_i ,
\tag{19.6}\]
where \(\alpha_k \sim N(0, 0.3^2)\) is a state effect and \(\nu_i \sim N(0, 1)\). The true effect is 0.3. In the notation of Equation 19.2, the shocks \(g\) are the 50 thresholds and the predetermined variables \(w\) are the incomes and states. Poorer people are more often eligible and have higher errors, so eligibility is correlated with the error through income and OLS is biased upward. The thresholds are drawn independently of incomes and errors, so Equation 19.2 holds.
Expected eligibility \(\mu_i\) is the probability that person \(i\) is eligible over the possible thresholds, holding income fixed. It is the share of the four thresholds above their income: 1 below 0.5, 0.75 between 0.5 and 1, 0.5 between 1 and 1.38, 0.25 between 1.38 and 2, and 0 above 2. It depends on income only, because every state draws from the same four values. Given income, the recentered treatment \(x_i - \mu_i\) moves only with the draw, which is why it is exogenous. A person with income 1.2 has \(\mu_i = 0.5\). The instrument is 0.5 if their state drew 1.38 or 2 and −0.5 if it drew 0.5 or 1, with equal chance whatever their error. People below 0.5 or above 2 always have zero and carry no identifying variation.
We compare four estimators, all with standard errors clustered by state.

OLS of \(y_i\) on \(x_i\). This is the same as instrumenting \(x_i\) with itself, the best predictor without recentering. It is biased.
The simulated instrument of Currie and Gruber (1996). They apply each state’s rules to one fixed national sample and use the share of that sample who would be eligible as the state’s instrument. The same population is run through every state’s rules, so the instrument measures the generosity of the rules and not the composition of the state’s residents. Here the national sample is all 10,000 people, and everyone in a state gets the same value. It is valid.
The recentered treatment, instrumenting \(x_i\) with \(x_i - \mu_i\). It varies within states, among people whose income lies between the lowest and highest thresholds. It is valid.
OLS of \(y_i\) on \(x_i\) and \(\mu_i\). Instrumenting \(x_i\) with \(x_i - \mu_i\) while controlling for \(\mu_i\) reduces to this regression (Borusyak and Hull 2026, footnote 8), so it is the controlled form of 3. It is valid.

The Monte Carlo is design-based. We generate the people once: their incomes, states and errors are the same in every replication. In each of 1,000 replications we draw new thresholds for the 50 states, recompute eligibility and outcomes, and fit the four estimators. The only randomness across replications is the policy draw, which is what the identifying assumption treats as random, so the spread of the estimates across replications measures each estimator’s precision under that design. The people and the 1,000 × 50 thresholds are stored as CSVs so the Julia companion computes the same numbers.


Code
people = CSV.read("data/recenter_people.csv", DataFrame)
draws  = Matrix(CSV.read("data/recenter_policy_draws.csv", DataFrame)[:, 2:end])
pool = [0.5, 1.0, 1.38, 2.0]
beta_true = 0.3
mu    = [mean(v .< pool) for v in people.income]   # expected eligibility
gener = [mean(people.income .< t) for t in pool]    # state generosity

function coef_x(f)
    i = findfirst(==("x"), coefnames(f))
    return coef(f)[i], stderror(f)[i]
end

const CL = Vcov.cluster(:state)
function one_draw(r)
    thr = draws[r, people.state]
    d = copy(people)
    d.x     = Float64.(d.income .< thr)
    d.y     = beta_true .* d.x .+ d.eps
    d.z_sim = gener[[findfirst(==(t), pool) for t in thr]]
    d.z_rc  = d.x .- mu
    d.mu    = mu
    fits = (feols(d, @formula(y ~ x), vcov = CL),
            feiv(d, @formula(y ~ 1), endo = :x, inst = :z_sim, vcov_type = CL),
            feiv(d, @formula(y ~ 1), endo = :x, inst = :z_rc, vcov_type = CL),
            feols(d, @formula(y ~ x + mu), vcov = CL))
    r2 = [NaN, cor(d.x, d.z_sim)^2, cor(d.x, d.z_rc)^2, NaN]
    return [collect(coef_x(f)) for f in fits], r2
end

R = size(draws, 1)
est = zeros(R, 4); se = zeros(R, 4); r2 = zeros(R, 4)
Threads.@threads for r in 1:R               # one slot per draw, race-free
    cs, r2[r, :] = one_draw(r)
    for j in 1:4; est[r, j], se[r, j] = cs[j]; end
end

DataFrame(estimator = ["OLS", "Simulated instrument", "Recentered treatment",
                       "OLS controlling for mu"],
          mean     = round.(vec(mean(est, dims = 1)), digits = 3),
          sd       = round.(vec(std(est, dims = 1)), digits = 3),
          coverage = round.(vec(mean(abs.(est .- beta_true) .<= 1.96 .* se, dims = 1)),
                            digits = 3),
          first_stage_R2 = round.(vec(mean(r2, dims = 1)), digits = 3))

The table gives each estimator’s mean and standard deviation over the 1,000 replications, the share of clustered 95% intervals that contain 0.3, and the average first-stage \(R^2\). OLS averages 0.637 against a true 0.3, and its intervals never contain 0.3. The three other estimators are centred on 0.3, with coverage of 92.7% to 93.7%, slightly below 95% with 50 clusters. They differ in precision. The simulated instrument has a standard deviation of 0.167 and a first-stage \(R^2\) of 0.26. It gives everyone in a state the same value, so it cannot separate people whose eligibility depends on the threshold from people who are eligible, or ineligible, under every threshold. title: 19  Recentered Formula Instruments
text:
19.4 The China shock
In ADH the shocks are at the industry-period level: the growth of Chinese imports into eight other high-income countries, per US worker, in 397 manufacturing industries over 1990–2000 and 2000–2007. ADH argue they are exogenous because the growth came from China’s side, through reform, rising productivity and WTO accession, and because imports into other countries do not respond to US demand. The argument is weaker for demand or technology shocks shared by all rich countries, and the identifying variation is concentrated in a few industries such as computers, toys and audio equipment (Goldsmith-Pinkham, Sorkin, and Swift 2020).
All four regressions below use the same instrument and differ only in what they control for. The treatment, US import exposure per worker, is shares times US import growth, and US imports also reflect US demand. Replacing them with the other-country shocks gives the prediction, which is the Bartik instrument itself, so the formula-instrument approach does not change the instrument. It changes the control. The shares, lagged employment shares in the 722 commuting zones, are incomplete, so the expected instrument \(\mu_\ell\) varies across zones, and controlling for it is equivalent to subtracting it. Its form depends on the shock design.

Design 1: the 397 shocks are exchangeable within each period. Every industry then has the same expected shock, the period mean \(\bar g_t\), which is 4.8 in the first period and 17.3 in the second, and Equation 19.4 gives \(\mu_\ell = S_\ell \bar g_t\). Only a zone’s manufacturing intensity is treated as predictable.
Design 2: the shocks are exchangeable only within each of the 20 two-digit SIC sectors in each period. Each industry’s expected shock is its sector’s mean \(\bar g_{mt}\), and \(\mu_\ell = \sum_m S_{\ell m} \bar g_{mt}\), where \(S_{\ell m}\) is the zone’s share in sector \(m\). A zone’s sector mix is also treated as predictable: a zone heavy in electronics is expected to receive a large instrument.

ADH control for the start-of-period manufacturing share with one coefficient for both periods, which approximates design 1’s \(\mu_\ell\). The second row drops that control, so nothing recenters the instrument, and it is valid only if the shares are exogenous. All fits use ADH’s other controls, census-division effects, population weights and standard errors clustered by state, with the GPSS replication files.


Code
adh = CSV.read("data/adh_master.csv", DataFrame)
tr  = CSV.read("data/adh_shares_triplets.csv", DataFrame)
shk = CSV.read("data/adh_shocks.csv", DataFrame)

function by_row(v)                          # sum over industries, by zone
    out = zeros(nrow(adh))
    for (r, x) in zip(tr.row, v); out[r] += x; end
    return out
end
sector  = string.(shk.sic87dd .÷ 100, " ", shk.year)
g_bar_m = Dict(s => mean(shk.g[sector .== s]) for s in unique(sector))

adh.B    = by_row(tr.share .* shk.g[tr.col])
adh.S    = by_row(tr.share)
adh.S_t2 = adh.S .* adh.t2
adh.t2n  = Float64.(adh.t2)
adh.mu2  = by_row(tr.share .* [g_bar_m[sector[c]] for c in tr.col])

controls = term(:l_sh_popedu_c) + term(:l_sh_popfborn) + term(:l_sh_empl_f) +
           term(:l_sh_routine33) + term(:l_task_outsource) + term(:t2n) +
           fe(:division)
function iv(extra)
    rhs = isempty(extra) ? controls : sum(term.(extra)) + controls
    feiv(adh, term(:d_sh_empl_mfg) ~ rhs, endo = :shock, inst = :B,
         weights = :weights, vcov_type = Vcov.cluster(:statefip))
end
fits = ["Bartik, ADH controls"               => iv([:l_shind_manuf_cbp]),
        "Bartik, no manufacturing control"   => iv(Symbol[]),
        "Bartik, design 1 mu (S x period)"   => iv([:S, :S_t2]),
        "Bartik, design 2 mu (sector means)" => iv([:mu2])]
DataFrame(specification = first.(fits),
          estimate = [round(coef(f)[1], digits = 3) for f in last.(fits)],
          se       = [round(stderror(f)[1], digits = 3) for f in last.(fits)])

The first row reproduces ADH’s −0.596: an increase in import exposure of $1,000 per worker over a decade lowers the manufacturing employment share by about 0.6 percentage points. Without the manufacturing-share control the estimate is −0.712.
Each of the last two rows removes one source of variation. ADH’s estimate partly compares zones with more and less manufacturing across the two periods: because the mean shock more than triples, a manufacturing-heavy zone gets a much larger instrument in the second period whichever industries China hit. Controlling for design 1’s \(\mu_\ell\) removes that comparison, and the estimate falls to −0.267 (0.087). ADH’s control is close to \(S_\ell\), with a correlation of 0.92, but one coefficient cannot absorb a term whose slope more than triples between periods. Design 2 also removes the comparison across sectors, such as electronics and toys against food and paper, and the estimate falls to −0.144 (0.117).
Whether the removed comparisons are confounded is the substantive question. If manufacturing-heavy zones declined faster in the 2000s for other reasons, such as automation, the design 1 control is needed and ADH overstate the effect. But the average shock is itself part of the China shock, since Chinese imports rose across nearly all of manufacturing. Designs 1 and 2 treat that average as predictable and use only the variation in which industries China hit harder than average, so they cannot measure an effect that works through manufacturing as a whole. ADH’s −0.596 does use it, and it is valid if the shares are exogenous given the controls. The data cannot tell us which assumption holds. Every estimate is negative, and recentering shows how much of the size depends on the assumption.

title: 19  Recentered Formula Instruments
text:
19.5 The Medicaid application
Borusyak and Hull (2026) instrument Medicaid eligibility in the 2014 ACA expansion with actual minus expected eligibility, treating expansion as random within the governor’s party. The first-stage partial \(R^2\) rises from 0.01 to 0.80 over the simulated instrument and the standard error on crowd-out falls by 44%. Most of the gain comes from the 18% of the sample whose eligibility the expansion could change; outside it, the recentered instrument is zero, and in the full sample without an exposure control it is less precise than the simulated one (Borusyak and Hull 2026, Table A4). Their 2012–2013 placebo on private insurance is −0.011, half the main estimate of −0.023 (Table A2).

title: 19  Recentered Formula Instruments
text:
19.6 Spillovers: deworming
Miguel and Kremer (2004) study a deworming programme in 75 primary schools in Busia, Kenya. The schools were listed alphabetically within strata and assigned in turn to three groups of 25, which started treatment in different years. Worms spread between children, so treating one school can lower infection at schools nearby. To measure this, they count the pupils at treated schools within 3 km of each school, and they control for the total number of pupils within 3 km.
Let \(D_j\) be 1 if school \(j\) is treated, \(n_j\) its number of pupils, \(p_j\) the probability that it is treated, and \(j \sim i\) mean that \(j\) is another school within 3 km of school \(i\). The spillover exposure of school \(i\) and its expected value are
\[
x_i = \sum_{j \sim i} n_j D_j, \qquad \mu_i = \sum_{j \sim i} n_j p_j .
\tag{19.7}\]
The shocks \(g\) are the assignments, and the predetermined variables \(w\) are the locations and pupil counts. Assignment is random, but a school in a dense area has more treated neighbours in every draw. If density also affects the outcome, through crowding or sanitation, the exposure is correlated with the error. In the first year one third of the schools were treated, so \(p_j = 1/3\) for every school and \(\mu_i\) is one third of the total pupils within 3 km. Miguel and Kremer’s total-pupils control is therefore the recentering. The exposure is the treatment itself, as eligibility was in the simulation, so the estimator is OLS controlling for \(\mu_i\), estimator 4 above. If the treatment probability differed across schools, for example by stratum, the control would have to be \(\mu_i\) and not the total pupils.
A second simulation checks this in a district like Busia. We place 75 schools in a 30 km by 30 km district, half around a town and half spread over the rest, and give each about 400 pupils. In each draw exactly 25 schools are treated, so \(p_j = 1/3\). Let \(N_i\) be the total pupils at other schools within 3 km and \(\eta_i \sim N(0, 0.05^2)\) a school error. The outcome, school participation, is
\[
y_i = 0.05 D_i + 0.03 x_i - 0.02 N_i + \eta_i ,
\tag{19.8}\]
with \(x_i\) and \(N_i\) in thousands of pupils. Treatment raises participation by 5 points at the school and by 3 points per thousand treated pupils nearby. Schools in dense areas have lower participation for other reasons. As before, the schools, their pupils and errors are fixed, and the 1,000 replications redraw which 25 schools are treated. We regress \(y_i\) on \(D_i\) and on (a) \(x_i\), (b) \(x_i - \mu_i\), or (c) \(x_i\) and \(N_i\), with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.
To see what goes wrong without the control, take two untreated schools whose neighbours each have 400 pupils, and treat each neighbour independently with probability 1/3. School A is in town and has three neighbours within 3 km, so \(N_A = 1.2\) thousand and \(\mu_A = 0.4\). School B is rural and has one neighbour, so \(N_B = 0.4\) and \(\mu_B = 0.133\). The number of A’s neighbours treated is binomial, so the exposures take these values:

Each school’s expected exposure is its exposure averaged over the draws, weighted by their probabilities. For A,
\[
\mu_A = \frac{0 \times 8 + 0.4 \times 12 + 0.8 \times 6 + 1.2 \times 1}{27}
= \frac{10.8}{27} = 0.4 ,
\]
which is the 1.2 thousand pupils nearby times the treatment probability 1/3. For B, \(\mu_B = 0 \times 2/3 + 0.4 \times 1/3 = 0.133\). The town school expects more treated neighbours because it has more neighbours. In the most likely draw A has one treated neighbour and B has none. With \(\eta_i\) set to zero, Equation 19.8 gives
\[
y_A - y_B = 0.03 (0.4 - 0) - 0.02 (1.2 - 0.4) = 0.012 - 0.016 = -0.004 .
\]
A has 0.4 thousand more treated pupils nearby and participation 0.4 points lower, so the comparison suggests a spillover of about −0.01 per thousand, when the true value is 0.03. The density gap, which is the same in every draw, is attributed to exposure.
The formula instrument uses \(x - \mu\), how lucky each school was relative to its own expectation, as the instrument for \(x\):
\[
\hat\beta = \frac{\text{cov}(y, x - \mu)}{\text{cov}(x, x - \mu)}, \qquad
\text{cov}(y, x - \mu) = 0.03 \, \text{cov}(x, x - \mu) - 0.02 \, \text{cov}(N, x - \mu) .
\]
The second term is zero. \(N\) is fixed for each school, and each school’s \(x - \mu\) averages zero over its draws; for A, \((-0.4 \times 8 + 0 \times 12 + 0.4 \times 6 + 0.8 \times 1)/27 = 0\). The ratio is then exactly 0.03. Raw \(x\) does not have this property, because A’s exposure is high in most draws and A is the dense school. Pooling all draws of the two schools with equal weight, the covariance of \(x\) with \(N\) is 0.053 and the variance of \(x\) is 0.089, so the slope of \(y\) on \(x\) is \((0.03 \times 0.089 - 0.02 \times 0.053)/0.089 = 0.018\). The covariance of \(x - \mu\) with \(N\) is 0, and the formula instrument gives 0.03.
With 75 schools and one draw, the covariance of \(N\) with \(x - \mu\) is close to zero but not exactly zero, which is the extra noise of estimator (b). Controlling for \(N_i\), which here is the same as controlling for \(\mu_i\), removes the density term exactly. The comparison is then between schools with the same number of pupils nearby, which is why (c) is tighter.


Code
schools = CSV.read("data/deworm_schools.csv", DataFrame)
treat   = Matrix(CSV.read("data/deworm_draws.csv", DataFrame)[:, 2:end])
ns = nrow(schools)
near = [i != j && hypot(schools.east[i] - schools.east[j],
                        schools.north[i] - schools.north[j]) < 3
        for i in 1:ns, j in 1:ns]                # within 3 km
N  = near * schools.pupils ./ 1000             # total pupils nearby, thousands
mu = N ./ 3                                    # expected treated pupils nearby

function one_assign(r)
    D = Float64.(treat[r, :])
    x = near * (schools.pupils .* D) ./ 1000
    d = DataFrame(D = D, x = x, N = N, x_rc = x .- mu,
                  y = 0.05 .* D .+ 0.03 .* x .- 0.02 .* N .+ schools.eta)
    fits = (feols(d, @formula(y ~ D + x), vcov = Vcov.robust()),
            feols(d, @formula(y ~ D + x_rc), vcov = Vcov.robust()),
            feols(d, @formula(y ~ D + x + N), vcov = Vcov.robust()))
    return [(coef(f)[3], stderror(f)[3]) for f in fits]
end

R = size(treat, 1)
dw_est = zeros(R, 3); dw_se = zeros(R, 3)
Threads.@threads for r in 1:R               # one slot per draw, race-free
    for (j, (b, s)) in enumerate(one_assign(r))
        dw_est[r, j], dw_se[r, j] = b, s
    end
end

DataFrame(estimator = ["(a) Exposure, no control", "(b) Recentered exposure",
                       "(c) Exposure, control for nearby pupils"],
          mean     = round.(vec(mean(dw_est, dims = 1)), digits = 3),
          sd       = round.(vec(std(dw_est, dims = 1)), digits = 3),
          coverage = round.(vec(mean(abs.(dw_est .- 0.03) .<= 1.96 .* dw_se, dims = 1)),
                            digits = 3))

Without the control, the spillover estimate averages −0.024 against a true 0.03, and its intervals never contain 0.03. Dense schools have more treated neighbours and lower participation, and the regression assigns that gap to the spillover. Both recentered versions are centred on 0.03. Regressing on \(x_i - \mu_i\) alone leaves \(-0.02 N_i\) in the error, so its standard deviation is 0.038, about twice the 0.020 of (c). Neighbouring schools share that error and the same treated schools, so the robust intervals of (b) contain 0.03 only 43% of the time. With the control for nearby pupils the remaining error is independent across schools, and coverage is 92%.

title: 19  Recentered Formula Instruments
text:
19.7 Summary
Shift-share is one formula instrument, with the formula and the design fixed by convention. Any formula of shocks and exposure is valid once its expected value over the shock design is subtracted, and the most efficient formula is the recentered best prediction of the treatment. Applied to Bartik, this has two consequences. When the shares do not sum to one, the regression must control for the sum of shares times the period’s mean shock. When the treatment depends on the shocks through more than shares times shocks, a prediction built from the treatment’s own formula is a stronger instrument than Bartik. In the ADH data the first consequence alone moves the estimate from −0.60 to −0.27. The same logic covers spillovers. A school’s expected exposure to treated neighbours is the treatment probability times its nearby pupils, which is the control Miguel and Kremer used.
For the shift-share construction, the share and shock views, and inference, see the previous chapter, Shift-Share Instrumental Variables.

title: 20  IV in Poisson with Fixed Effects
text:
20.1 The model and setup
Poisson regression specifies the conditional mean as an exponential function: \[E(y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \exp(\mathbf{x}\boldsymbol{\beta})\]
As a quasi-maximum likelihood estimator (QMLE), Poisson regression requires only that the conditional mean is correctly specified; the true count distribution does not need to follow a Poisson distribution, and standard errors are easily made robust to arbitrary overdispersion or heteroskedasticity.
However, when an explanatory variable is endogenous—correlated with unobserved omitted factors—standard linear two-stage least squares (2SLS) intuition fails. Because the conditional mean is nonlinear, unobserved confounders enter multiplicatively inside the exponential function.
This chapter covers:
Let \(y_1\) denote the count outcome, \(y_2\) the endogenous explanatory variable, and \(\mathbf{z} = (\mathbf{z}_1, \mathbf{z}_2)\) the vector of exogenous variables (\(\mathbf{z}_1\) included in the structural equation, \(\mathbf{z}_2\) excluded instruments).
The structural conditional mean is: \[E(y_1 \mid \mathbf{z}_1, y_2, c_1) = \exp(\mathbf{z}_1\boldsymbol{\delta}_1 + \alpha_1 y_2 + c_1) \tag{20.1}\]
where \(c_1\) is an unobserved omitted variable correlated with \(y_2\). Our primary estimand of interest is \(\alpha_1\), the structural semi-elasticity of \(y_1\) with respect to \(y_2\).

Two departures from Wooldridge’s notation are maintained for clarity: 1. Wooldridge writes the coefficient on \(y_2\) as \(\gamma_1\); we write \(\alpha_1\) to align with standard treatment effect notation. 2. Where Wooldridge writes \(\mathbf{x}_1\boldsymbol{\beta}_1\), we write \(\mathbf{z}_1\boldsymbol{\delta}_1 + \alpha_1 y_2\).


20.1.2 Fixed effects in the exponential model
Everything below absorbs fixed effects without comment, and it is worth saying once why that is allowed. Fixed-effects Poisson has no incidental parameters problem (Wooldridge 1999; Lin and Wooldridge 2019). With \(N \to \infty\) and \(T\) fixed, the unit effects enter multiplicatively, factor out of the score, and are conditioned out cleanly. The estimator of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is consistent even though the number of unit parameters grows with the sample. Probit and logit have no such property, which is why the first stage of Section 20.3.4 needs the Mundlak device while the second stage does not.
The software follows from this. In Stata, xtpoisson, fe fits the conditional model, but the community standard is ppmlhdfe (Correia, Guimarães, and Zylkin 2020): it absorbs several dimensions of fixed effects at once, it is fast, it detects separated and singleton observations, and it recovers predicted values with the absorbed effects put back. In Julia, Panelest.jl provides fepois() for the same job, with feols() for the linear first stage.
Stata’s ivpoisson handles endogenous regressors, but it cannot absorb high-dimensional fixed effects. That is the practical reason the panel literature routes endogeneity through a control function rather than through a packaged IV command: the control function leaves the second stage as an ordinary FE Poisson regression, which ppmlhdfe and fepois already do well.

title: 20  IV in Poisson with Fixed Effects
text:
20.2 Control functions and GMM

20.2.1 A linear second stage: the control function is 2SLS
To see where the nonlinear complication begins, consider first the linear model: \[y_1 = \mathbf{z}_1\boldsymbol{\delta}_1 + \alpha_1 y_2 + \varepsilon_1, \qquad E(\mathbf{z}'\varepsilon_1) = \mathbf{0}\]
Two-stage least squares (2SLS) replaces \(y_2\) with its linear projection \(\hat{y}_2 = \mathbf{z}\hat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}_2\): \[y_1 = \mathbf{z}_1\boldsymbol{\delta}_1 + \alpha_1 \hat{y}_2 + (\varepsilon_1 + \alpha_1 \hat{v}_2)\] where \(\hat{v}_2 = y_2 - \hat{y}_2\) is the OLS residual.
Alternatively, the control function (CF) approach decomposes the structural error \(\varepsilon_1\) via a linear projection on the first-stage residual \(v_2\): \[\varepsilon_1 = \rho_1 v_2 + \eta_1\] where \(\rho_1 = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon_1, v_2)}{\mathrm{Var}(v_2)}\). By the properties of linear projection, \(E(v_2 \eta_1) = 0\) and \(E(\mathbf{z}'\eta_1) = E(\mathbf{z}'\varepsilon_1) - \rho_1 E(\mathbf{z}'v_2) = \mathbf{0}\).
Plugging this into the structural equation yields the augmented regression: \[y_1 = \mathbf{z}_1\boldsymbol{\delta}_1 + \alpha_1 y_2 + \rho_1 \hat{v}_2 + \eta_1\]
By the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (FWL) theorem, OLS estimation of this augmented regression produces an estimate \(\hat{\alpha}_1\) that is numerically identical to 2SLS. No additional distributional assumptions are required beyond the standard orthogonality condition \(E(\mathbf{z}'\varepsilon_1) = \mathbf{0}\).


20.2.2 A nonlinear second stage: the control function needs more than uncorrelatedness
When the conditional mean is exponential, this automatic numerical equivalence breaks down.
Substituting the error decomposition \(c_1 = \rho_1 v_2 + e_1\) into Equation 20.1 yields: \[\begin{aligned}
E(y_1 \mid \mathbf{z}, y_2, v_2) &= E\left[ \exp(\mathbf{z}_1\boldsymbol{\delta}_1 + \alpha_1 y_2 + \rho_1 v_2 + e_1) \mid \mathbf{z}, y_2, v_2 \right] \\
&= \exp(\mathbf{z}_1\boldsymbol{\delta}_1 + \alpha_1 y_2 + \rho_1 v_2) \cdot E\left[ \exp(e_1) \mid \mathbf{z}, y_2, v_2 \right]
\end{aligned} \tag{20.2}\]
For the augmented index \(\mathbf{z}_1\boldsymbol{\delta}_1 + \alpha_1 y_2 + \rho_1 v_2\) to correctly specify the conditional mean in a Poisson second stage, the remaining expectation factor must be strictly constant: \[E\left[ \exp(e_1) \mid \mathbf{z}, y_2, v_2 \right] = \text{constant}\]
This is why Wooldridge (2010) (sec. 18.5) normalizes \(E[\exp(e_1)] = 1\) rather than \(E(e_1) = 0\).
This condition restricts the conditional moment-generating function of \(e_1\) at a single point. Every moment of \(e_1\) enters it, so it is far stronger than the zero-covariance condition that suffices in the linear model. It is not, however, an independence condition. Independence of \(e_1\) from \((\mathbf{z}, v_2)\), together with \(v_2 \perp \mathbf{z}\), is a sufficient assumption that delivers it, and it is the assumption we maintain below because it is simple to state and is what the standard derivation uses. Any weaker restriction that holds \(E[\exp(e_1) \mid \mathbf{z}, y_2, v_2]\) constant would serve equally well.
